An analysis of data from LHCb LHC collisions at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies has yielded 7753 $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ event observations. By comparing these events to 4 million simulated $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ events, a decay duration of $0. five million years$ was calculated, consistent with $0. five million years$ expectations and $1.3 sigma$ tighter.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of wide-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics.

The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a centre of mass energy of 5.02 TeV and 25 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, enabling a comparison with interpolated pp measurements at 2.76 and 7 TeV. Owing to its sophisticated design and reliability, the ATLAS detector successfully collected a comprehensive dataset during heavy ion and proton-proton runs. As a result, it facilitated precise measurements of various particle distributions that weren't previously accessible, alongside the nuclear modification factor in p+Pb collisions, which demonstrates the detector's capabilities and provides valuable information for further developing its capabilities.

This paper discusses the application of Lie algebras in quantum mechanics, specifically focusing on how the principles of quantum mechanics are implemented for systems whose configuration spaces are parameterized by the Lie algebra's dimension, of either $A_{n}$, $B_{n}$, or $C_{n}$. We also explore the method of generating quantum operators from the classical Poisson brackets and examine the effects of a noncommutative parameter on the harmonic oscillator. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the spin-and magnetic field-controlled harmonic oscillators. Additionally, we present the solution to the problem of quantizing the Yang-Baxter map, previously studied in [RB14, RB19], and show that the quantum operators obtained in this manner match those derived from the Poisson-Norden theorem.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze medical images on a range of devices, from high-end computers to more basic systems. Specifically, we tried training a number of models to analyze the infiltration of lymphocytes in cancer tissues, using a dataset consisting of 3000 images collected from various sources. We compared the results of training models both with and without data from these diverse sources, using models that had been pre-trained on a range of datasets. Our experiments showed that training on a smaller dataset led to better performance when the models were trained independently, but not when they were trained jointly. Additionally, we found that training on a larger dataset didn't significantly improve performance when the models were trained independently, but it did with federated learning. Notably, we also discovered that using models that had been pre-trained on other datasets didn't improve performance when the models were trained independently, but it did with federated learning.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge when it comes to batch normalization. To overcome this, we've developed a method called Pruning in Time (PIT), which optimizes TCNs by pruning dilations while resetting normalized values. Through extensive experimentation on six benchmark datasets across three categories, our model demonstrates superior performance, averaging 12.5% improvement in accuracy with only 6.5% increase in parameters.

This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific property: solvability. As a result, its nilpotent subalgebras are automatically solvable. We also establish that the solvability aspect is a distinguishing characteristic of the Zinbiel algebra itself, separate from its nilpotent subalgebras.

This study offers initial evidence for transverse flow angle fluctuations in lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, based on data collected by the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider. To analyze this data, a statistical approach was utilized, providing first measurements of flow angle and flow magnitude fluctuations. The results show increased kurtosis of the distribution of flow angle and magnitude, indicating that the flow distribution is more skewed than predicted by the hydrodynamic model, particularly in mid-central collisions. This study also reveals that the fraction of elliptical flow attributed to initial conditions increases with centrality, exceeding 80% in the most central collisions.

Previously, we established a common connection between various DLE-logs based on the isomorphism between BBI-frames and R-EBI-frames. Building on this connection, we now identify an unified inverse operator for the DLE-logs in question, specifically $\Box_\mathcal{L}^\downarrow$. This unified operator is grounded on the link between BBI-frames and R-EBI-frames, and as such, it links $\Box_\mathcal{L}^\downarrow$ to the corresponding SCC-opera.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional dependencies. Unlike conventional approaches that require a complete and consistent dataset to define data integrity constraints, our work allows these constraints to be specified even before data is entered, or even if the data contains null values. We also consider a scenario where some data entries may conform to multiple depen-dencies. We have developed algorithms to resolve inconsistencies by finding the most minimal corrections needed to restore data consistency, or one of several optimal solutions if multiple minimal fixes exist. We demonstrate the limitations of our approach in handling certain complex scenarios, such as equational unions, and show that inconsistent datasets with nulls and functional dependencies have a more extensive coverage than their counterpart with only nulls and foreign keys. Additionally, our research explores applicable data scenarios and assesses the performance of our methods with real-world data.

This study presents a novel dynamic statistical model called Poisson Autoregressive, which models time-varying counts based on past values and a constant trend. Unlike conventional AR models that assume a fixed relationship between variables, this model detects changes in this relationship over time. A notable feature of this model involves the use of a score test for structural breaks, which identifies changes in the parameter values without specifying their time of occurrence. Additionally, the model can be expanded to accommodate multiple breaks, offering a comprehensive framework for analyzing data with complex patterns of change.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
bridges the gap between object detection and field representation. NDFs are
three-dimensional, symmetric, and comprehensive object representations that
incorporate both geometric and semantic information. We propose the NDF, which is
based on a SE(3)-equivariant network and can be learned from point clouds or
meshes, allowing it to be easily integrated with existing object detection
frameworks. To validate the NDF, we design the 3D Semantics Holistic Field
Benchmark, a challenging, comprehensive evaluation platform that assesses an
object's entire presence and details. On this benchmark, our approach,
NDF-descriptor, a combination of the NDF and a descriptor field, achieves
exceptional performance by accurately identifying and detailing objects on the
MUCO-24 dataset and extensively evaluating other NDF-based methods.

The SiD Detector is one of the leading designs for the future ILC research, representing a comprehensive approach to precise particle physics investigations. As the status of the ILC remains uncertain, it's essential to explore alternatives in case the detector isn't optimized for the experiment's needs. Therefore, this presentation will review the proven principles of the SiD Detector and discuss adjusted design options for the calorimeter system and the central magnetic field, considering potential impacts on performance and cost.

We performed a detailed analysis of the globular cluster Tononzintla 2 (Ton 2) utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy for nearly 2000 stars affiliated with the cluster, including 24 satellites of the Gaia mission's bulge fields in CAPOS (Carlos Aceituno, P.I.): N1-N4 and B1-B4. These new observations allowed us to precisely determine the cluster's motion, distance, and key astrophysical characteristics. Notably, we found a relatively young age of 5.56 ± 0.11 for Ton 2, consistent with other clusters at the galaxy's core, and a metal content of -1.55 ± 0.10, a value slightly more negative than comparable globular clusters in the Milky Way. The cluster exhibits a higher rotation velocity of approximately 24.0 ± 2.0 km/s, exceeding typical galactic globular clusters by a significant margin. Additionally, we identified a small offset of -2.6 ± 0.6 in the [Fe/H] value for the oxygen abundance of Ton 2, indicating a slight deficiency in oxygen compared to other stars within the cluster. This finding might be an early indicator of external interactions affecting the cluster or more broadly, the galaxy's core.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, offering numerous specifications of theoretical computer science concepts, but creating an overall understanding still proves challenging. A comprehensive analysis of the archive's content is undertaken in this research, focusing on the overarching framework consisting of high-level specifications and low-level proofs. A new, improved framework is developed and incorporated into the archive, demonstrating its utility and user-value through the incorporation of a new example. Additionally, both the original and the new framework are made publicly available in the FFormals repository, facilitating collaborative analysis and contributions.

Using the functional renormalization group at the edge of the Yang-Lee domain, we have analyzed the behavior of the Yang-Lee edge singularity in O(N) universality classes. We have determined that the position of this singularity, as expressed as the ratio kI/l, follows a specific value regardless of the number of components N, except in the case where N equals zero. Additionally, our results indicate that the amplitude of the density of zeros near the Yang-Lee edge varies significantly with N. Furthermore, we have established that the critical exponent associated with the Yang-Lee edge singularity can be calculated using the amplitude of the density of zeros. Our calculations for the shift in the edge's position and the amplitude of the density of zeros provide valuable insights for the theoretical evaluation of the Yang-Lee edge singularity using the functional renormalization group.

In statistics and machine learning, it is common to make assumptions about a random variable's distribution in order to make inferences about its properties. Under these conditions, it is frequently possible to make precise predictions about certain variables' behavior. The goal of this study is to provide a detailed analysis of how these predictions are made and to explore whether similar methods could be applied to a broader class of models that share some key characteristics. The model in question makes predictions about a set of interconnected random variables based on their individual characteristics and their interactions with each other. The study demonstrates that these predictions are accurate when the variables' values are relatively close to their expected values and that they do not rely on the specific distribution of the variables. It is possible to make similar predictions about a broader class of models that share some key characteristics with the model in question. The study also explores whether the predictions it makes about one of these models are reliable when the model in question makes assumptions about the distribution of a set of interconnected random variables based on their individual characteristics and their interactions with each other.

Modern wireless communications are experiencing exponential growth, yet the availability of spectrum is limited, making frequency allocation extremely precious. To optimize usage, researchers and industry leaders are investigating novel transmitters and receivers that can multiply the available spectral bandwidth, enabling smoother development. Such technology is known as an electromagnetic nonreciprocal converter (ENRC), which can transmit information in a specific frequency range even if a signal is applied in a different range. Enabling the creation of compact, low-loss ENRCs would be a significant breakthrough. Recently, metal-dielectric stacks with unique properties known as metamaterials have shown great potential in the field of electromagnetics, and researchers are now exploring the potential of these materials to develop ENRCs. This study simulates a metal-dielectric stack consisting of periodic copper layers surrounded by ferromagnetic material, which exhibits distinct properties known as isotropic gyromagnetic response. To understand these properties, the study uses different simulation methods, including general simulation and a method that focuses on specific components. The findings suggest that the converter could potentially transmit 5 GHz signals using a relatively small magnetic field. However, further experimentation is needed to validate the results.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth fully integrable vector fields at points where the field's underlying flow exhibits topologically conservative behavior. As a key aspect, we demonstrate that near points where the flow's underlying Poincaré map displays conservative dynamics and has a rational critical point, there exists an arbitrarily smooth local orbital linearization for the associated vector field. This research builds upon earlier proofs by Pugh, Putnam, and Fassler-Putnam.

This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained data derived from Complete Configuration Interaction 1-electron density functions, the eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. For example, it achieves nearly 99% accuracy in predicting energies for the first energy levels of the hydrogen-like isotopes of beryllium, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and neon, which have atomic numbers ranging from 5 to 10. Additionally, the eCPNN model demonstrates its capability to describe rotational symmetry in the ground state of helium-4. Unsupervised training with configuration interaction density functions is also possible using a method called constrained training, which leverages the density function of a lower energy level as a reference. This yields more precise predictions for higher energy levels. Furthermore, the eCPNN model can be applied to describe instantaneous interactions within nuclei, as demonstrated with a simplified example, and its potential to contribute to the development of new approaches to studying electron correlations is explored.

The Advanced Camera for Surveys on HST has provided high-resolution, multi-object imaging capabilities that have significantly improved our understanding of the universe. With its large and versatile field of view, ACS has enabled extensive investigations of massive structures in the universe. In a study involving nearly 3000 ACS images, our team has, for the first time, thoroughly examined HST's coverage of the sky, and has identified an enormous warm-area deviation in the constellation of Centaurus. This deviation stems from a massive arc formed by gravity, created by a massive and distant galaxy acting as a lens, and has the distinctive characteristic of being composed of multiple distinct images. Due to the position of the lensing galaxy and the direction of HST's line of sight, this arc appears as a massive, elongated structure in the optical range. As a result of this unique perspective, this phenomenon was only detectable in HST's optical spectrum, and not in HST's near-infrared view. As HST continues to observe this particular region of the sky, its data will provide critical insights into the behavior of this lensing galaxy, and its effects on the surrounding environment.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the interpretation of these cues using traditional methods. We classify two-stage pipelines into two sub-groups based on the type of intermediate cues used: coordinate maps and projection images. We also sub-categorize coordinate map based pipelines into two further sections: simple projection and complex projection. In the latter section, assumed presence of low-frequency background in real-world images is considered. In this work, we focus on simple projection based pipelines and proposed novel architecture, DeepHMap++, which learns correspondence relationships between image pixels in stage one and uses a modified projection clustering method in stage two to estimate the object pose. We also introduced enhanced projection clustering (EPCL) framework that learns correspondence between a point and other point projections at one dimension and extended EPCL as high-dimensional projection clustering (HD-EPCL) framework that learns correspondence in n-dimensional space. We utilized HD-EPCL in our proposal DeepHMap++ and implemented it through public dataset and achieved superior results compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, several suggestions are made on how to further advance bond-based peridynamic models through the incorporation of fluid dynamics and multi-phase modeling capabilities.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on existing methods, GGLasso incorporates established
algorithms including AMEN, Quickest, RD-GLasso, and SARAH for structured graphs,
along with novel techniques like Quickest with node-wise splitting and
approximate solutions for large-scale and sparse graphs. The library offers users
flexibility in choosing solution approximations and exploitation methods for
structured graphs and is accompanied by efficient tools for evaluating algorithm
performance. GGLasso is tailored to handle large-scale and sparse graphs and
leverages Numpy and Scipy for computational efficiency. The library can be
downloaded from https://github.com/ga79/GGLasso.

A new method has been proposed for sampling configural space without assumptions about molecular potential energy surfaces. By combining an extensive set of quantum chemical calculations with meaningful motion within the configurational space, the method enhances efficiency and effectiveness for challenging chemical problems. A theoretical framework and two practical applications demonstrate the benefits of this approach, showing that it can achieve superior results compared to traditional methods in less computational time.

Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. Therefore, a significant task involves identifying the appropriate configuration for the binary system and its environment at this point in the process. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. It's also been found that if matter is directly overlaid onto a binary system, without properly considering the potential for matter to influence the binary's motion, this leads to inaccurately calculated orbital paths due to artificial factors, rather than a signature of dark matter at play. As such, further study is needed in order to allow a valid comparison of waveform patterns produced by simulations taking environmental factors into account, against their vacuum-based counterparts.

We investigate the spectral stability of a specific star-shaped graph, consisting of three equal branches, within the framework of the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation. Our analysis focuses on the spectral properties of the equation's Dirichlet L^2 operator on this star-shaped graph. It is demonstrated that when the number of divisions between the branches exceeds 3, there is a distinct, exponentially damping eigenvalue mode present. Conversely, when the number of divisions is 2 or 1, the spectrum becomes continuous and unstable. Furthermore, our findings are verified by numerical examples, involving the computation of eigenvalues and mode plots for various division counts.

Researchers demonstrated a novel sonic lens material based on rubber-like polymers to improve photoacoustic imaging. The sonic lens enhances the acoustic properties of a given material without altering its optical characteristics, allowing for accurate imaging. It was shown that a specific sonic lens variant, made from a particular silicone mixture, significantly reduces photoacoustic signal loss and improves image clarity, even with low-energy lasers. The technique was successfully tested on phantom models and real breast tissue. The findings suggest that photoacoustic tomography using a silicone sonic lens can achieve high-quality images with lower energy levels, reducing the risk of tissue damage. Furthermore, the method enables clear imaging of deeper tissue layers.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance. In these networks, composed of various interconnected layers, the value of a node's centrality depends on the centrality of its connected nodes, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality. Distinguishing our approach from existing variants is the consideration of distinct relationships between nodes in different layers, allowing us to use a parallelised algorithm based on the RASPA framework. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through applications to ranking nodes in multi-layered networks and identifying influential spreaders in multi-layered networks for diffusion processes.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking in low-light raw images directly, combining deblurring, demosaicking, and denoising into a single joint task. To achieve this, we devise a novel raw-image model that integrates demosaicking, tailored to produce color images from noisy raw data. This model is based on a simple and effective extension of existing raw-image models, utilizing a mosaic-based residual representation to capture mosaic-pattern constraints. By doing so, we show that demosaicking can be learned as an integral part of noise reduction, eliminating the need for explicit demosaicking steps. Moreover, our results demonstrate superior performance when compared to standard processing pipelines and state-of-the-art raw-to-image models that apply separate demosaicking steps.

This research aims to examine the behavior of a massless particle moving at light speed within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, which is derived from f($R$) gravity. The associated metric variation leads to a non-Flat spacetime metric. We then derive the Dirac equation within this altered spacetime framework using the metric variation approach. Due to the presence of a scalar potential, we find that the energy levels and wave functions are significantly affected compared to their flat spacetime counterparts. Specifically, we find that the energy levels are no longer continuously quantized as in flat spacetime but rather take the form $n\hbar c = \sqrt{3}l_{P} \sqrt{n^2E^2 - (E/3)}$ where $l_P$ is the Planck length, and we observe that the wave functions develop an additional oscillatory component. Moreover, we predict the energy split between two energy levels of a particle and an antiparticle, given by $\Delta E \approx (4/3)\hbar^2/(l_P)^2$. This difference in energy could potentially be measured in high-energy particle physics experiments.

The Causal Learning category in Machine Learning has been undergoing substantial advancements, enabling the development of systems that can make informed predictions and take strategic actions based on their experience. However, a significant hurdle in these systems exists, as they are only as reliable as the accuracy of their training data, and they lack the ability to systematically explore their environment to discover valuable insights about the underlying causal relationships that shape it. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called the Causal Exploration Toolbox, which utilizes a range of techniques such as mutual information optimization, active learning, and causal discovery, enabling causal relationships to be uncovered through proactive observation and interaction with the environment. We test this approach on both simple symbolic worlds and complex real-world environments, and our results show that it outperforms traditional methods based on performance-only optimization in both cases.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions.

We analyze a set of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories in the presence of a generalized theta-term. This term is produced by the reduction of the four-dimensional Chern-Simons term in Type IIB supergravity and results in a relation between the axion and the dual field of one of the gauge fields. This relationship can lead to the creation of a potential energy term that breaks global symmetries, specifically those associated with an $SU(2)\times SU(2)$ group. However, this effect can be avoided if the charge of the axion under one of the $SU(2)$ groups is zero. The general relation we establish also applies to Type IIB compactifications that involve anti-branes, which introduce a charge that can result in the breakdown of global symmetries.

Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications, which necessitate running security applications on separate hardware components to function properly. This paper introduces an innovative method for hardware partitioning, which minimizes the amount of trust needed from the operating system and reduces potential vulnerabilities. Through a case study of a single-core smartphone, we present a novel hardware-isolation design that utilizes a separate, low-capability CPU for insecure tasks, allowing the secure CPU to handle sensitive operations. This design showcases an affordable and easily-implementable approach to reducing trust, which involves moving insecure tasks to the low-capability CPU via software emulation. Experimental results indicate that this approach has minimal performance impacts, making hardware partitioning an appealing solution for mobile device owners.

Reinforcement learning is increasingly used to improve energy efficiency in network management, but its application is hindered by high networking costs and significant data corruption. The issue lies in the fact that current reinforcement learning methods require extensive exploration before determining an optimal policy. To overcome this limitation, we develop a novel data-efficient approach called the Resilient Policy Gradient (RPG) algorithm. By recognizing that corrupted data is distinct from zero-shot data and typically follows a separate distribution, we leverage the fact that the two can be distinguished through the use of a separate neural network controller. The RPG algorithm takes advantage of this distinction by filtering out corrupted samples and selecting action embeddings from a separate distribution. As a result, RPG achieves significantly better performance compared to existing methods, with an average improvement of 143% in our experiments.

We uncover an unselectable version of the box game paradox, featuring players making remarkably accurate predictions of unknown real numbers without access to relevant information. Additionally, our analysis confirms the requirement of choice in solving the classic problem and examines alternative configurations of the game.

Our experiments reveal subtle orbital selection in cubanite's electrons, with some electrons preferring higher-energy orbitals further from the center, while others are more comfortable in lower-energy ones closer to the center. This effect is strengthened by cubanite's pressure, which causes the electrons to shift their preferences, resulting in differences in the movement of electrons in the material's conductivity and absorption of light. Our findings are supported by calculations using strong-coupling theory, which shows how the interaction between the electrons and vibrations in cubanite influence the selection of orbitals.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-quantum-bit interference, is driven by the growing availability of two-dimensional materials and advanced experimental setups. Interferometry with multi-quantum-bits offers an precise measurement of a system's overlap function, whereas interference between macroscopic quantities provides a massive enhancement in sensitivity. Although previous research has focused on systems with external magnetic fields, our findings reveal significant fluctuations in the dark exciton state without the need for magnetic fields, making possible the creation of large-scale, field-free quasi-one-dimensional quanta that exhibit immense Rabi oscillations. Our approach incorporates a novel approach, involving the application of circularly polarized laser light in small angles, which results in the interaction of dark excitons with nearby quasi-one-dimensional states. This method enables the formation of a massive, two-dimensional superposition state that exhibits immense Rabi oscillations, as confirmed by our experimental and theoretical findings. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of this approach to develop sophisticated quasi-one-dimensional quantum devices, such as the implementation of a quantum gate operation relying solely on the interaction with a nearby quantum state.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic network from a non-symmorphic wallpaper pattern, where a 2D lattice with hexagonal and square domains is connected through a reciprocal relationship. We are examining the band structure of this network with a 2D tight-binding model, incorporating hoppings across adjacent domains and at domain boundaries. Our analysis reveals a tunable Dirac point by adjusting the strength of these inter-domain hoppings. Initially, we establish that a singular Dirac point appears within the highest energy branch of the band structure. Then, we demonstrate that by adding a specific relation between the hoppings within and across domains, we can shift this singular point to the conduction band, creating a pair of degenerate Dirac points. These findings open up possibilities for experimenting with Dirac points in a lattice that can be synthesized with chalcogel materials exhibiting large atomic spacings.

Building on the concept of catalysis in quantum optics, a single-photon catalyst can facilitate the creation of coherent states from a specific input, thereby enabling the generation of exotic states that were previously catalysis-dependent. A novel approach is proposed to efficiently produce these catalyzed coherent states using a combination of quantum transformations and the control of multiphoton states. A particular example is demonstrated where a single-photon catalyst, formed through the interaction between a quantum state of light and a nonlinear medium, can transform a specific input state into a Schrödinger cat state. The proposed method also offers a way to study the properties of catalytic transformations in quantum optics.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the distinct algebraic types of the Weyl tensor. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, beginning with a review of the basic properties of bivectors and their connection to the infinite-dimensional conformal group. The conformally invariant quantities, such as the conformally invariant 4-tensor constructed from the bivectors, are then examined. The process of converting bivectors to Newman-Penrose coefficients is demonstrated, along with an exploration of the infinite-dimensional conformal group's representation in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. The review also explores the relationship between the Newman-Penrose coefficients and the infinite-dimensional conformal group, revealing that the latter can be expressed as a linear combination of the former. The review concludes with an examination of the Weyl curvature index, often referred to as the Ricci degree, which can be determined using the Newman-Penrose formalism and bivectors.

A new technique for identifying polymer structures given the molecular mass and functional group count has been developed. By organizing specific functional groups into three distinct categories based on polymer chain length, and utilizing a systematic approach to cover all possible polymers, a solution framework has been established. This framework first calculates the number of units in each type of functional group by determining the most likely value for each, either exactly or within a certain range. Given that certain values are known exactly, others must be calculated or estimated with the use of linear regression. A case study has been created to demonstrate the applicability of this technique and an analysis of the results has been performed.

Optimizing systems with complex dynamics through trial and error is not an efficient approach, especially when the task is to achieve a high-level objective that may not be directly measurable. This paper introduces a sophisticated technique called direct transcription optimization, which transforms the time-domain problem into an algebraic one by using numerical integration to replace differential equations. This method allows the incorporation of nonlinear constraints, making it ideal for addressing challenging dynamic systems. However, the technique requires a detailed understanding of its underlying principles and cannot be implemented through standard optimization tools. Consequently, the technique's potential benefits are not fully realized by the broader control systems community. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to direct transcription optimization, along with a case study on a critical system during the COVID-19 pandemic, to illustrate its applications and opportunities for further research.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method using a DDAUnet model, which seamlessly integrates data, architecture, and optimizer settings to maximize performance. By fine-tuning the model with esophageal tumor data from public sources, we found it could accurately detect and outline tumors with high precision and recall rates. Notably, this involves modifying the dense connector and dense block components of the network to focus on specific texture types, which are critical for detecting tumors. Moreover, we discovered that our model generalizes well to datasets it has not seen before, successfully detecting and outlining tumors in CT scans from multiple sources with similar levels of precision and reliability. These results suggest that doctors can trust the output of this automatic system and integrate it into their clinical assessment, reducing the need for additional information.

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date reservoir models derived from well log analysis. For such applications, the models used should account for uncertainty and variability in the data, a task that proves challenging for the traditional approach. In this paper, we combine an ensemble of conventional well log analysis methods to facilitate real-time geosteering and generate reservoir models that incorporate the inherent uncertainty of well data. Our approach utilizes multiple types of static and dynamic data to constrain the formation evaluation process and estimate property distributions through modeling uncertainty. In one real-world example, we compared the results of our method to an existing approach, achieving better matches between calculated and actual reservoir data using our combined approach. Furthermore, our method enables the generation of static and dynamic constraints for geosteering, facilitating decision-making during the drilling process.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, despite the intrinsic hierarchical nature of the task. In contrast, we propose integrating nested NER into a paradigm of comprehensive structure parsing, leveraging a systematic approach to parse the structural aspects of language. Furthermore, we introduce the Refined Label Parsing Model (RLPM), a model that systematically generates complex NER structures in a holistic manner. RLPM consists of two components: a nested NER module and a subsequent entity schema normalization module. We evaluate RLPM on the Wiki59C dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance in almost twice as many cases as the current top-ranking model without the benefit of character-level information.

We examine a family of smooth plane quartics with four analytic markings, along with the corresponding bitangents. Contrary to previous knowledge, we find that the moduli space of these plane quartics, when counted with sign, as we pass to an equivalent family of tropical quartics, becomes the space represented by the Gram matrix of a specific 4-dimensional lattice. We further establish that this space has a significant relation to the representation of another 4-dimensional lattice, and that this connection explains the rationality of the original space. This analysis involves an $\mathbb{A}^1$-counting technique that allows us to determine the cardinality of the plane quartics' birational representations. Additionally, our results provide the basis for investigating the real signed count of these plane quartics.

Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative algorithm suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks utilizing time difference of arrival (TDOA) data, which takes into account the interference that often occurs when different technologies are used. The algorithm's performance is evaluated under various interference levels in simulations. The outcomes suggest it outperforms existing methods, especially in scenarios characterized by moderate to heavy interference, where a significant reduction in error rates can be achieved.

Code-mixed languages, which involve the combination of two or more languages within a single medium, are becoming increasingly prevalent due to the growth of social media and online interaction. This development poses a significant challenge to traditional monolingual approaches in NLP. As a result, Code-Mixed NLP has emerged as a promising new field, focused on developing effective solutions for code-mixed language data. However, numerous obstacles need to be addressed to support multilingual societies, and several intriguing patterns within code-mixed data present opportunities for further exploration. This paper examines three intriguing aspects of code-mixed data, including the evaluation of code-mixed models, the identification of language switches, and the comprehension of code-mixed text. By delving into these topics, the paper aims to encourage researchers to engage with code-mixed data and explore the many benefits that code-mixed NLP can offer.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. While systems are often improved using these descriptions, they are usually provided without the underlying images. Human-provided ratings for the accuracy of generated descriptions against actual images are proposed as a more effective evaluation method. Unlike previous methods, this approach directly assesses the systems' ability to describe images correctly, rather than their ability to mimic training data. It is demonstrated that describing images for human raters is a more challenging task than creating new training examples, and this method is used to evaluate and compare the performance of several image description systems.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_3$O$_5$, Ta$_2$O$_5$, or TaO$_3$, have been extensively simulated using first-principles methods, and these calculations have revealed that all three formulas are possible equilibrium states depending on the oxygen pressure. We have also used Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase transitions between these formulas, and our results indicate that Ta$_2$O$_5$ should be TaO$_3$-like at high oxygen pressures, Ta$_3$O$_5$-like at middle pressures, and $\beta$-Ta$_2$O$_5$-like at low pressures. Notably, these calculations are in agreement with experimental X-ray diffraction data, and we have analyzed the electronic and optical properties of these formulas as well.

The spread of misinformation on social platforms poses a significant challenge, exacerbating the existing concerns of manipulating elections through online disinformation. To tackle this issue, researchers need to identify the circulating false information to be warned or counter it. In this study, false rumors are modeled using a Bayesian method that accounts for limited data availability, as well as user feedback, to estimate the percentage of users who have seen the false information. A novel approach, the Shift Model, is introduced to capture the significant phenomenon of geographic information dissemination patterns changing significantly around Election Day in the United States. The model's components highlight the regular circulation patterns of misinformation before the election, the sudden disruption of these patterns, and the difference in circulation trends across different geographic regions.

We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection tool called LDoR, designed to identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data environments, particularly emphasizing its applications in financial surveillance systems. As information flows quickly, current methods like conventional statistical analysis or machine learning techniques prove insufficient due to their limitations in handling rapid data changes. In contrast, LDoR utilizes a cutting-edge, model-based approach that builds on theoretical foundations, offering a clear and transparent understanding of anomalies. This approach leverages latent variables to pinpoint unusual incidents and, thanks to its computational simplicity, enables timely detection of anomalies in complex data sets, even in rapidly evolving environments. The development of LDoR is illustrated through a practical example involving the analysis of complex healthcare data, and its advantages are showcased by comparing its performance to that of widely used machine learning methods.

Humans teach industrial robots through demonstration, relying heavily on speech to clarify any issues that arise during the demonstration process. If communication is limited to text-only, it would significantly reduce the efficiency of their training. Understanding the speech used in these situations is crucial to enhancing their training. This study focuses on analyzing the speech patterns used by human instructors as they demonstrate robotic tasks by providing verbal explanations of key action components, dubbed "manipulation primitives." It investigates the acoustic characteristics of these primitives using both a speech analysis tool and a machine learning approach, resulting in classifications of speech based on their primal forms, spatial characteristics, and grammatical structures. It also explores the relationship between the acoustic features and semantic meanings of these primitives, using both a learning approach and a statistical analysis. It ultimately reveals that some classification is possible by primality, but not by spatial characteristics or grammatical structures, and finds that certain features stand out in certain primitives. It then demonstrates the benefits of primitive-based modeling in speech, showing that it leads to better classification and more accurate interpretation of speech. It concludes that enhancing the acoustic qualities of low-primitive speech would have the greatest training benefits.

This paper introduces a random model for generating tree structures with various node types, where each internal node has a specific type and each leaf node is assigned a random type. The types are organized in a hierarchical structure, with some types being subtypes of others. The challenge lies in deriving a formula for the number of type-consistent trees within this framework. To accomplish this, the paper divides the analysis into several components, including counting the number of possible locations for internal nodes, based on the structure of the type hierarchy. It also explores ways to randomly assign leaf node types and develops a algorithm for constructing trees consistent with the type hierarchy. The paper ultimately presents an analytical formula and demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through numerical computations.

A special class of field theories, characterized by Euler-Arnold equations, is comprised of those whose underlying symmetries conform to conformal properties. This underlying mechanism is exemplified through the use of Lie algebras, leading to simplifications that result from the integration of symmetry-based principles, known as "infinitesimal methodology." However, this abstract conclusion omits the intricate mathematical details involved in this process, including the sophisticated recharacterization of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras and their derivative subalgebras, as well as the complex modifications applied to the Euler-Arnold equations to accommodate conformal properties.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing system for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances.

Using a sophisticated statistical method to analyze observations of the known planets in our solar system, we have conducted a precise assessment of the potential for detecting the gravitational impact of an unseen world, commonly referred to as Planet X. By utilizing high-precision measurements of the positions and movements of the planets obtained since 1976, our analysis has enabled us to confidently rule out the possibility of a highly elliptical, massive world with a diameter at least twice that of Neptune, at a distance of less than 3 astronomical units from the Sun. However, certain areas of the solar system remain difficult to detect, particularly higher-than-expected tilts of the solar system's plane, which could indicate the presence of a smaller, more closely orbiting world. Our research provides a statistical framework that can be applied to future astronomical observations, which are expected to significantly reduce the possible mass and orbital distance ranges for such a world.

Previous studies have demonstrated that neural machine translation models incorporating monolingual word embeddings can generate more natural language, but these models typically rely on learning monolingual lexicons during artificial training, which results in limited ability to translate unfamiliar words. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to neural machine translation that enables the model to draw upon a pre-trained monolingual lexicon memory, allowing it to translate words it hasn't encountered before. To achieve this, we modify the source language mask during translation to match the vocabulary used for monolingual word embedding development, effectively tying the model's source language to the monolingual vocabulary. We then train the model to select the monolingual word embeddings corresponding to the target word from the memory, thereby leveraging the pre-trained monolingual lexicon. Experimental results indicate that our approach significantly improves translation performance, particularly for low-frequency words and rare names, when using the BERT monolingual word embeddings and lexicon memory.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions.

This paper builds upon previous work of the second author with Daskalopoulos and Vazquez, which involved introducing an alternative approach to the Yamabe flow based on evolution equations. The paper presents a variation of this approach, specifically relating to the Yamabe flow on fractions $\Delta^u (u^1/n) + u^{1-n}$, with an initial condition $u_0$. The paper demonstrates that this new approach yields a well-posed problem in the sense of weak solutions, and further shows that this approach can be used to prove the convergence of the Yamabe flow on fractions $\Delta^u (u^1/n) + u^{1-n}$ to the Yamabe flow $\Delta u + u^{1-n}$, given that the initial condition $u_0$ satisfies certain smoothness requirements.

To tackle classification problems with a small number of labeled examples per task, few-shot learning has proven highly effective. However, traditional methods that rely on average models often struggle due to their limited robustness. In contrast, our proposed approach, which emphasizes learning from labeled examples through prototyping, demonstrates substantial improvement. By combining a prototype for each class with a background prototype, our method successfully accounts for instances that don't fit a particular class or are difficult to classify. The features of these prototypes are extracted using a feedforward network, and their classification is achieved via nearest neighbor comparison. Our method's benefits are showcased through its performance on miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

User behavior on multiple sparse domains (e.g., movie ratings and purchase history) exists for each user, and our goal is to develop a unified user profile that leverages this diverse data. Although previous approaches have succeeded in single-domain recommendations by processing complex user preferences, they often struggle when scaling to multiple domains due to limited information in each area. Additionally, existing multi-domain methods frequently overlook interactions between domains and settle for basic addition or weighted averaging techniques, resulting in an incomplete and unsatisfying user profile. To address these limitations, our proposed framework, Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR), employs a comprehensive aspect preference learning approach in order to create a unified user profile across multiple domains. In this approach, each domain contributes unique aspect preference learning components, while the underlying aspect taxonomy serves as a unifying framework, enabling cooperative learning and profile unification through taxonomic reasoning. Extensive simulations on real-world data demonstrate the superior performance of the MSDCR framework compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Convex optimization issues often take the form of conic equations, where various mathematical structures such as matrices with specific properties or vectors with particular characteristics can be linked together to define a convex cone. In this work, we present Hypatia, a Julia library designed for directly solving these individual structures, in contrast to using a generic convex optimization solver like CPLEX or Gurobi. By taking this approach, we can leverage the efficiency of specialized algorithms for particular types of convex objects, such as determinants of matrices, to our advantage. We demonstrate how Hypatia can be used to set up and solve a wide range of convex optimization problems involving various cones, including problems arising in multivariate regression, semidefinite programming, and matrix scaling, among others.

The escalating expense of neurology research scans and growing size of imaging datasets are prompting researchers to develop methods for quality assurance (QA) that rely on machine learning, using previously assessed data. However, training these models proves challenging due to the limited number of high-quality training images required for both QA and clinical use. Additionally, QA models need to account for several factors including patient safety, potential side effects of medical procedures, and regulatory compliance which are often assessed subjectively through standardized measures. Furthermore, these models must be able to handle diverse population demographics. 

We investigated the application of machine learning for automatic QA of brain MRI scans using a large, multi-center dataset of 17,000 scans from diverse population demographics. We developed and evaluated several models, taking into consideration various factors such as radiation risk, stroke, cardiac conditions, tumor type, surgery history, lesion type, and institutional performance, which were characterized as continuous or categorical features.

The results showed that a machine learning model performed significantly better than a random selection in choosing scans for a protocol. Moreover, these models achieved high accuracy in predicting certain features and somewhat lower accuracy for others. Furthermore, we discovered that certain features were highly protocol-specific, while others were less predictive and varied greatly in their prediction criteria.

The research revealed that certain features required further standardization and normalization to enhance predictability. Additionally, incorporating multiple, complementary imaging modalities was found to be beneficial in predicting certain features. 

Overall, our research demonstrated that machine learning can effectively generalize across

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the resilience of distribution networks, we developed a framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in a multi-agent optimization model. This framework effectively utilizes mathematical programming to minimize costs and maximize user satisfaction through optimal charging and routing solutions for private vehicles within a specific region. Furthermore, we demonstrated the efficacy of our approach by applying it to an actual urban setting, utilizing real-world data, and comparing it against a conventional method using fixed routing patterns. Our results showed that our approach yields more practical and resilient solutions.

Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) introduces a new type of non-volatile RAM that can be used as part of a system's main memory. To help assess its capabilities, we've incorporated the Optane DC PMM into our memory hierarchy evaluation framework. Initially, we observed the Optane DC PMM to behave similarly to solid-state drives (SSDs) in situations involving block-level accesses, but it performed like fast memory when accessing individual bytes. Consequently, its performance became optimal when it was directly integrated into memory. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the Optane DC PMM can significantly improve performance by reducing memory latency, eliminating the need for memory allocation, and combining the advantages of memory and storage. In addition, we discovered that the Optane DC PMM can efficiently support multiple processes accessing shared memory simultaneously. In certain scenarios, it even outperforms software caching.

In a collaborative scenario involving multiple agents, a key factor motivating action is likely the expectation of meaningful interaction with others. This study introduces a pioneering'meeting' framework for independent agents to come together and engage in reciprocal relationships. At the core of this framework is a novel 'drive-based' motivation mechanism, where an agent's desire to connect with others is fueled by internal 'drives,' which in turn trigger exploratory behaviors. As the meeting unfolds, recurrent patterns of behavior emerge as agents adjust their connections based on the advantages they bring. Key features of this framework include the generation of natural language dialogue grounded in cognitive and motor activities, all while ensuring the feasibility of the meeting. Demonstrating the framework's effectiveness, a series of experiments show that agents learn to optimize their connections and develop distinct personalities. Additionally, the potential of this meeting framework to model real-life scenarios is showcased through an exploration of driving-related conversations.

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications.

The paper makes predictions about the physical properties of newly proposed baryon and meson particles, based on existing theories. It predicts the masses of these particles, using two different mathematical frameworks: the Quark-Gluon Model and the Large $N$ Expansions with meson non-estractability theorem. It also makes predictions for the masses of baryon and meson particles composed of quarks and antiquarks that have not been previously assembled. Additionally, it makes predictions for the masses of particles composed of quarks and gluons, specifically diquark and triquark systems, which could potentially form meson-like and baryon-like particles, respectively.

In 1951, Gelfand and MacPherson established a fundamental linking theorem for the irreducible representations of the symmetric group in $k$ variables, $S_k$. This landmark result was subsequently generalized to the symmetric group $S_n$ by Friedlander and Losik in 1970, following which multiple generalizations were made. Here, our purpose is to broaden their result to the family of Coxeter groups of the B-type by generalizing the Friedlander-Losik result to these groups.

Utilizing a vast sample of Type Ia Supernovae from the Pantheon dataset, statistical distortions created by weak lensing are measured for the first time with such a large sample size. These distortions, which appear as an asymmetry in SN images, can be quantified through the average flux difference between the galaxy's major and minor axes. Our analysis reveals a significant correlation between this asymmetry and redshift, taking into consideration any potential biases introduced by the detection limits of SNe. Through a lensing model integrated with the effects of galaxy morphology, we are able to predict the expected asymmetry associated with weak lensing for a specific range of galaxy properties. Our findings match the expected outcomes of a lensing model, with a significant dependence on both SN's angular separation from lensing peaks and the distribution of lensing masses. Additionally, there is a significant relationship between asymmetry and SN's declination, which cannot be fully explained by a simple lensing model. Further analysis is needed to fully comprehend these correlations.

These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The main objective of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth explanation of the variational method for monotone and coercive stochastic partial differential equations. 

The necessary background on Hilbert space-based functional analysis, operator theory, and stochastic analysis has been recapitulated within the lecture notes and further relevant references are included. 

The concluding chapter covers the pathwise approach.

In photonic systems, tailored at subwavelength dimensions, we observe unique properties in silicon-on-insulator materials. To fully utilize these characteristics, we propose a method of creating notched structures within the photonic waveguide by integrating a lateral p-i-n junction. This structure enables the formation of subwavelength resonances and mode selection through the application of an electric voltage. By integrating a notched nanostructure into the photonic device, we achieve refined light emission properties, including reduced threshold voltages and increased electron beam stability. These improvements are attributed to the reduction of electric field penetration into the active region, demonstrating the potential of this design for solid-state emitter applications requiring minimal dimension sizes.

MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging capabilities, combined with sophisticated analysis techniques, enable detection of hard-to-spot tumors. This assignment delves into the fundamentals of image processing, introducing techniques such as Gaussian filtering, gradient analysis, region growing, and morphological analysis, while illustrating their application in identifying breast tumors via MRI images.

In this research, we explore the properties of a novel algebraic variant of the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$, as well as its corresponding degenerate Bernoulli number. This investigation is grounded in an innovative algebraic approach to degenerate polynomials and numbers, allowing for easy determination of various $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ properties. Our findings also reveal connections to well-known sequences like the Stirling numbers of the second kind and the degenerate Euler numbers.

The problem of stellar activity noise in spectroscopic stellar parameters and planetary mass estimation is highly significant. It affects measurements in various ways, depending on the technique and data used, especially when employing the surface distribution function to relate activity and parameters. While it masks the signal of low-mass planets, it also contributes to the scattering of uncovered planets. A method to reduce this noise by selecting specific line lists for least-squares deconvolution was investigated. The aim was to examine if it could increase the accuracy of parameter measurements and detect hidden planets, considering different activities in different spectral lines. Two approaches were tested: a parametric method based on the physical properties of line formation and a randomised method. The results showed that the line lists selected by the randomised method were able to reduce the scatter and bias in parameter measurements more effectively. Furthermore, using these line lists led to the detection of additional planets in two out of three analysed cases, with the model architecture contributing to this success. Consequently, developing an automated code to generate these line lists for any given data and technique is highly recommended.

This research paper proposes a new approach called HRPB-LQEC for adapting hierarchical collections in Wireless Sensor Networks to handle temporary connectivity issues and estimate the quality of links bi-directionally. Like existing hierarchical collection methods, HRPB-LQEC organizes nodes into hierarchical levels to reduce communication complexity, but it differs in its handling of intermediate levels and link quality estimation. Unlike other methods that ignore or simplify intermediate levels, HRPB-LQEC considers them crucial and develops a method to estimate link quality in both directions. The design of HRPB-LQEC is based on a virtual infrastructure concept called Virtual Collector Tree (VCT), which consists of a root, intermediate levels, and leaf nodes. Each node can act as an intermediate level, leaf node, or both, depending on its connection to nearby nodes. To function effectively, HRPB-LQEC utilizes a link quality estimation method called Bidirectional Qualities (BQs), which evaluates the quality of links in both directions and assigns a quality score to each node. To maintain the quality score, each node adjusts its behavior based on the result of BQs. HRPB-LQEC's performance was evaluated by simulating a network with varying numbers of nodes, different distances between nodes, and different levels in the network, and its results showed an average improvement of 24% in delivery ratio and 21% in network lifetime compared to existing collection methods.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the performance of each object detector on the
CityScape dataset, and our findings reveal that recurrent object detectors are
capable of learning from context, whereas transformer-based object detectors
have difficulty learning from context when the entire image is inputted, and often
require the assistance of auxiliary cues.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a version of the Moser-Trudinger inequality for a function with a nonhomogeneous growth condition and a type of concentration compactness leading to existence of solutions, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for multiple solution existence.

We establish new concentration inequalities for a set of dependent Bernoulli random variables that satisfy a stochastic dominance condition. Specifically, let X1,..., XN be independent and identically distributed random variables with expectations E[Xi] = p and var[Xi] = σ^2, and let Y be the sum of these variables, normalized by their mean and variance. Under the strict inequality p < 1/2, we derive a concentration inequality bound of the form P(|Y - Np| > t) ≤ 2exp(-t^2/(2Nσ^2)) for any t > 0. This improvement becomes significant as N increases. Additionally, our results extend to a broader category of random variables, including those with binary outcomes that satisfy a certain negative correlation property.

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Dieudonné theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and flat cohomology with torsion for schemes $X$ over $R$.

This study explores the double longitudinal spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, specifically focusing on the cosine distribution of the helicity of final observed hadrons. Using the amplitude expansion, particular attention is paid to the $\cos\phi_n$ asymmetry component. The connection between the helicity amplitudes of hadron polarization and the twist-2, 3 fragmentation functions is explicitly shown, and the interpretation of $\cos\phi_n$ asymmetry in the context of SIDIS is clarified. Furthermore, the theoretical calculation of the $\cos\phi_n$ asymmetry in SIDIS is performed, and it is found that positive and negative hadrons exhibit distinct behavior in this regard.

We've established recently, much like our work on Deformed Special Relativity, that Fock's coordinate transformation can be developed from a novel perspective involving the coherent state representation of the coordinate and momentum operators.  Deforming this perspective in conjunction with the de Sitter spacetime metric yields the deformed coordinate transformation.  This transformation can then be applied to the coherent state representation of the kinetic energy operator, leading to a mathematical expression that mirrors the structure of a harmonic oscillator.  By combining this harmonic oscillator-like expression with the mass term, we derive the energy spectrum for a particle in the de Sitter spacetime.  This process results in an energy eigenvalue equation expressed in terms of the Laguerre polynomial, in contrast to the initial expectation of a Heisenberg spin-half operator.  Additionally, we demonstrate that the energy spectrum is reachable via the unitary operator that relates the de Sitter spacetime metric to its flat spacetime counterpart, referred to as the Fock transformation.  Our research provides concrete evidence that this Fock transformation serves as a bridge connecting the deformed spacetime to its undeformed counterpart.

Quantum syrups, initially introduced in (GSW19), can be thought of as a partial version of the quantum switch circuit (MW18), which we refer to as the symplectic conversion of unitary matrix U, denoted as π_U. This conversion maps input state α |0+1| to β |1+0| via unitary U on combined qubits 0 and 1. A specific property of the symplectic conversion is that it preserves the maximum average value of the Bell function, which could be very helpful in developing approximate conversion methods.
