By investigating a range of $\alpha$-attractor inflation models, we found that in certain cases, where the field is in the dark regime, the relation we derived can result in an increased PBH creation rate due to perturbations in the congruence, exceeding the limit set by the gravitational potential well. Furthermore, we found that in some $\alpha$-attractor inflation models, where the field is in the dark regime, the standard gravitational wave generation mechanism may be overridden by the perturbation contribution, leading to a significant increase in the PBH creation rate, thus providing a potential explanation for the observed PBH population.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some nodes as deepest vertices. They were interested in determining the number of such trees given a specific number of deepest vertices, as well as proving a related recursive formula. In contrast, a contrasting problem involving unmarked ordered trees had a well-defined solution. By establishing a bijection between the two types of trees, they were able to use this existing information to find the answer to the first question.

This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of machine learning-based character recognition in extracting meaningful information from election ballot tallies. As part of this research, an Informed OCR (iOCR) system was developed to refine the existing OCR technology. To test the iOCR system's performance, a subset of election data from North Carolina was used. The study finds that the iOCR system outperforms traditional OCR technology, demonstrating an error reduction rate of 0.5-1.5 percentage points for each character on average. Additionally, the study includes a comparison of the iOCR system's performance in recognizing characters when ballots are printed in a particular font and when the font is varied.

In deep learning models, overparameterization is often paired with regularization to prevent overfitting. This study explores if this combination is necessary by investigating a linear time series modeling framework with multiple stochastic processes generating synthetic data. The analysis shows that, even without restricting model capacity through overparameterization, using L2-regularization is still effective in controlling benign overfitting. The research also finds that certain design aspects, such as varying the number of features and time series length, influence model performance. The findings are further validated on real-world data, demonstrating that the proposed approach yields better results compared to alternative methods.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper showcases a novel deep learning architecture, centered on a comprehensive attention mechanism within a bidirectional neural network framework. This innovative design deviates from traditional attention-based models that often apply complicated memory-based attention functions, whereas our proposal straightforwardly integrates attention into a simple bidirectional sequence-to-sequence model, bypassing the need for explicit memory components. Additionally, we've incorporated a bidirectional connection to facilitate mutual information exchange between forward and reverse propagation paths, enhancing the model's overall performance. Experimental results indicate our proposed framework, readily applicable to various deep learning platforms, outperforms existing reference models in terms of speech quality metrics.

A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack.

A key factor in microgrid operations is the capacity to store energy, but it also introduces new risks due to uncertainty in demand and pricing. This study examines how risk-averse decision makers self-allocate energy storage across different markets to maximize expected utility, taking into account storage limitations and transaction costs. We develop mathematical programming approaches to solve this problem efficiently and conduct numerical tests to validate our methods. The results show that risk-averse decision makers can benefit from allocating storage across different markets and that these allocations are sensitive to the level of risk aversion. Furthermore, we observe that in certain scenarios, the self-allocation of energy storage may lead to it being underutilized due to high transaction costs, and that grid connection costs can significantly impact the allocation of energy storage across different markets.

In quantum systems, superpositions of electronic states rapidly evolve, 
within the timeframe of few femtoseconds to attoseconds, leading to a charge 
density that varies over time. This work takes advantage of newly produced, 
ultrafast soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser to create 
an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the temporal evolution 
of core electrons over approximately 23 picoseconds, as a result of their mutual 
interaction. Corrections to this were made by considering the effects of the 
irradiating infrared pulses.  A combination of theoretical models and experimental 
findings reveal that, in a time frame of just a few femtoseconds to 10 femtoseconds, 
the electron cloud changes from a spherical to an elliptical shape, with its long 
axis directed perpendicular to the molecular bond. This means that in nitric oxide, 
as with other biatomic molecules with a bond length shorter than 6 angstroms, the 
electrons exhibit this elliptical shape, whereas in nitric oxide, this occurs due to 
core-hole vibration rather than electron wave packet dynamics.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

Large-scale multi-task learning is a widely observed phenomenon in deep learning, where many models exhibit better performance when trained on fewer larger images as opposed to more smaller images. This research aims to understand this phenomenon by comparing various training schedules at a large ImageNet scale. The study considers four scenarios: training one dataset at a time, training all datasets simultaneously, training a subset of the datasets in parallel, and sequential training of the datasets. The results indicate that sequential training achieves the highest accuracy among the methods studied, reaching an 5% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet validation set. Moreover, the findings suggest that the key factor influencing performance is not the size or distribution of the training data but rather the elimination or retention of valuable knowledge during training. The research also introduces a simple technique, called Dynamic Learning, to manage knowledge retention during training. The code and the dataset split used in this research are publicly available for download.

This paper departs from the conventional view of studying the spectrum's algebraic multiplicity by instead examining its geometrical interpretation in the context of algebraic varieties. The underlying variety's invariance under a key transformation simplification leads to a critical insight that significantly contributes to the study's results. The relationship between certain spectral properties and the geometry of the variety is determined by using the studied results. The theory is illustrated through a self-contained example. Lastly, the paper's findings are applied to an underlying problem of the Schur complement computation.

We suggest creating pairs of correlated bosonic states within long-lived dipole molecules interacting with an optical cavity. This system can be used to develop an optical-squeezing-based detection method for homodyne measurements of optical phase. Building on previous work, we now incorporate two new key features: first, pair creation is driven by the application of a coherent light pulse rather than a laser, second, we demonstrate that this approach leads to the efficient generation of squeezed states. We provide theoretical guidelines for optimizing this process, including selecting the optimal duration and frequency of the pair creation pulse. Furthermore, we propose a method for determining the squeezing parameter in our system.

Researchers who utilize silicon-based quantum computing platforms need a more in-depth comprehension of electron-electron interactions. By integrating two electron spin states within a single $^{28}$Si atom, it's possible to utilize the quantum property of entanglement to enhance quantum processing unit performance. To accurately model this system, a new method has been developed that utilizes a large basis set and a multi-valley effective mass approach. This method ensures energy accuracy within 0.1 eV when compared to complex CI simulations. It allows for the examination of donor arrangements in silicon in a more efficient and systematic way. By running this model through a supercomputer, a vast dataset of donor configurations was created and made available for public use. This dataset includes information on energy levels, probabilities, and transition matrices. It can be utilized to enhance the development of silicon-based quantum sensors and quantum processing units.

Our investigation focused on the conductance of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac spectrum. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were considered, with different types of boundary conditions applying to them. When boundary conditions are oriented perpendicular to the electric field, we found that the conductance is a minimum, compatible with a non-quantized value (0.02e^2/h) for large samples, derived from helicity-scattered carriers. In mesoscopic samples, with boundary conditions varying between zero and one, the conductance linearly changes, correlating with the number of holes released from the zero-energy level. This understanding is reinforced by experimental measurements showing varying conductance levels corresponding to different quantum states. Additionally, our study explores the implications of boundary conditions on the one-dimensional edge states that emerge in mesoscopic samples.

Roadside safety has been a pressing concern for mobile communication systems, which are prone to catastrophic failures due to their long distance between vehicles and the speed at which information is transmitted. To address this issue, a significant amount of research has focused on applying non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) to vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications, which have revealed that certain existing protocols are ineffective, particularly those that fail to account for dynamic changes in road conditions. In this paper, we introduce an novel, self-adjusting cooperative NOMA (ANC-NOMA) protocol designed to mitigate these issues. This new protocol works by continuously monitoring and assessing connectivity, which triggers a continuous process of optimization and adjustment. Our simulations have shown that ANC-NOMA achieves a 90% success rate in critical junctions, surpassing existing CC-NOMA and DC-NOMA protocols by 20% and 30% respectively. Furthermore, ANC-NOMA exhibits enhanced performance to 80% success rate in heavy traffic conditions and 90% in low-light environments, outperforming CC-NOMA by 25% and DC-NOMA by 35%.

In our proposed approach, we develop a mathematical model that schedules operations for an dynamic time division duplexing system in a 5G environment. Our model is based on a non-cooperative game and is used to maximize an operator's revenue. We also derive an analytical solution for the model's equilibrium point and provide a scheduling algorithm termed the 'LTDD scheduler'. This algorithm is efficient, dynamic, and systems-wide in its approach to scheduling. We evaluate the LTDD scheduler's performance under various system load scenarios and show through numerical data that it achieves near-optimal results.

An analysis of a Hall anomaly in YBCO has been successfully replicated by incorporating the effects of moving vacancies in a fixed lattice of vortices, and their interaction is quantified using new parameters that are determined from BSCCO thin-film data. This model highlights the significance of vacancies in understanding Hall anomaly, and it reveals that the predicted vortex vacancy binding energies and densities in the ab-plane match the values obtained from other studies. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the predicted vortex vacancy binding energies and densities in the c-axis direction differ significantly from the values obtained in the ab-plane, and this discrepancy is attributed to the distinct behavior of vortices in these directions.

Using experimental data from magnetic measurements in the Ising model's critical region, researchers previously found a consistent fixed point characteristic for all moments of the order parameter. To further investigate this phenomenon, new analysis is presented for the moments of the order parameter's distribution in the 3D Ising region, specifically for higher-order moments (fourth order and above). These results also reveal that all moments share the same universal behavior at the critical point, exhibiting a fixed point that reflects the distribution's characteristic in the 3D Ising region.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares that generate a type of subfactor known as a factor is well-known. However, when the square does not equal the identity, as is the case with this particular kind of subfactor, a characterization has yet to be achieved. In the context of this study, a square that commutes with a specific type of matrix is referred to as a square that "commutes with it in the standard way." This research focuses on identifying all the squares that commute with a given square in the standard way, especially those that also have the property of being hermitian. It is discovered that all such squares can be characterized as a specific type of matrix, as long as they commute with the given square in the standard way. In addition, this characterization holds true even if the square does not equal the identity. Building on this result, this research further characterizes all the squares that commute with a given square in the standard way, as long as they are also unitary. It is discovered that all such squares can be characterized as a specific type of matrix, as long as they commute with the given square in the standard way. This characterization holds true even if the square does not equal the identity. Furthermore, this research characterizes all the squares that commute with a given square in the standard way, as long as they are also hermitian. In this work, we examine the capability of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HamNNs) to acquire derivatives of input functions. To accomplish this, we suggest a new architecture that extracts a suitable canonical transformation, allowing for the computation of a specific derivative. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this architecture on synthetic and real-world data, finding that it efficiently yields accurate results compared to a counterpart model using standard neural network architecture. Additionally, we uncover the capacity of HamNNs to learn derivatives through the discovery of an underlying mathematical principle. Finally, we highlight potential applications of HamNNs in computing explicit profiles of ordinary differential equations and imply the potential for these networks to address more complex problems.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing users' confidence in it. A framework is proposed that includes multiple agents working together, one of which is a data expert that develops new, relevant data to supplement existing information, while another is a scoring expert that creates a trust metric for the model's predictions. These scores help refine the model's performance and boost the trust it inspires. Since the predictions and score calculations are made continuously, we need a way to update the model quickly. We use the score information to remove sections that aren't trusted, aren't certain, or don't match real data, thereby preventing the incorporation of biased data. The model's performance is improved over time by combining the predictions of a constant group of predictions. We test this approach with a simple example, removing predictions that aren't certain or match real data.

Detecting prohibited items in an x-ray image of luggage is crucial for ensuring public safety. However, the difficulty of interpreting image content for non-experts and the time they spend on examining images are significant concerns. As a result, it's essential to automate prohibited items detection in x-ray images. We've assembled a diverse group of experts and gathered their findings to create a high-quality benchmark consisting of x-ray images of 10 prohibited items and 1 background class. To further improve the accuracy of automated systems, we've developed the Lateral Inhibition Module, which effectively locates objects by preventing the system from focusing on irrelevant details. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of this module over existing techniques and its integration with efficient feature extraction leads to state-of-the-art performance on our newly created benchmark.

We create a new class of polynomial invariants for linked loops in a thickened torus, drawing from the ideas of Kauffman and Lusczek-Taylor. This invariant, named $\tilde{X}_{\lambda}$, is a modification of the semi-simplistic version of a superpolynomial in an extended version of the volume hypothesis. To develop $\tilde{X}_{\lambda}$, we use the extended volume hypothesis to establish relationships among various colored versions of the Kauffman polynomial. As a result, $\tilde{X}_{\lambda}$ exhibits volume hypothesis behavior and outperforms other invariants like the Kauffman and Jones polynomials in accuracy, especially in regions representing loop volume. Additionally, $\tilde{X}_{\lambda}$ yields distinct values for distinct loop configurations, indicating it is an exhaustive loop invariant. To streamline computation, we also present an efficient algorithm for $\tilde{X}_{\lambda}$ in a simplified form. Furthermore, $\tilde{X}_{\lambda}$ has a direct connection to the loop volume, which can be expressed using $\tilde{X}_{\lambda}$. We also introduce an expanded version of the volume hypothesis that establishes relationships among various colored versions of the Kauffman polynomial and prove it with an example focusing on the $n$-colored version.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing bileletal networks, have led to significant progress in this area, with several successful applications reported. However, most existing methods fail to consider three crucial factors: the contextual background, the structure of the input sentence, and the knowledge stored in a knowledge base associated with the word sense. To address these limitations, we propose a context-gloss enhancement network that incorporates contextual background, sentence structure, and knowledge base information to improve the accuracy of WSD. This multi-modal network, where the input comprises three components (context and gloss), allows the context and gloss to flow freely during neural network processing. Notably, our approach is versatile and can support various context and gloss representations, as well as multiple knowledge base formats. Experimental evaluations of the proposed system on three WSD datasets show its superiority over state-of-the-art baseline models.

This paper formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a specific regularization. Additionally, it presents related, regularization-dependent integral expressions of the gamma function.

This paper investigates top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions at 13 TeV and above, using the large acceptance and sensitivity of the LHC, specifically with the CMS detector. We examine the capabilities of forward proton tags and forward neutron plus proton tags for top quark pair detection, considering events with an electron or muon at the mid-gap, and above all, in presence of dense nucleon fields. We find that even with the most stringent cleanliness requirements, the signal to background ratio can reach 0.4-0.5 for forward proton tags and 0.08-0.1 for forward neutron plus proton tags. Furthermore, with advances in pile-up treatment and jet substructure, the signal to background ratio can be increased to 0.7-0.8 for forward proton tags and 0.15-0.2 for forward neutron plus proton tags.

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL tasks, specifically schema and value prediction, and introduces a novel framework to separate these elements from each other. The framework leverages an auxiliary task to enhance semantic interpretation across domain boundaries. During training, a single model combines task-specific and auxiliary tasks for both supported and unsupported domains. After training, this model can accurately handle unsupported domains. To validate our approach, experiments were conducted on the Spider dataset, a representative text-to-SQL benchmark, and the results show that our method outperforms the baseline in both supported and unsupported domains. Additionally, we discovered that our approach's performance can be further improved by incorporating a named entity recognition auxiliary task, and this improvement holds true even for supported domains.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy (DP) on networks, focusing on private analysis of network data and published studies on the subject. We examine various DP techniques applied to graph-related functions and discuss recent research on private network learning. Additionally, we address practical implementation challenges associated with DP on networks, specifically encountering obstacles related to DP on trees. Finally, we outline significant difficulties in the field and potential future research directions for network differential privacy.

The vast image database and comprehensive cosmic coverage of Euclid's nutritional segmentation maps will have a significant impact on the field of astrophotometry, allowing for detailed studies of galaxies, the Milky Way, and nearby stars. By analyzing these images, scientists can build advanced image processing algorithms, effective cosmic removal techniques, and precise estimations of photometric zero points. Furthermore, the evaluation of image quality will have a significant impact on spacecraft and instrument design, optimizing the performance of future cosmic explorers.

In this research, we propose an automatic method to generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create Bezier curves, we define the parameters of a virtual world in which the vehicle can operate. To identify potentially dangerous situations on this road network, we use a method that simulates the vehicle's movement along the planned route. By searching for optimal control points within a predetermined range, we create a variety of challenging road networks suitable for evaluating the limits of autonomous lane-keeping systems. Our approach has been successfully applied to a high-speed highway scenario.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist.

Researchers have successfully used quantum hydrodynamics to model non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel approach that directly generates random quantum hydrodynamic descriptions for interacting Bose gases. This method eliminates the need to specify a specific quantum hydrodynamic description and instead enables the creation of random descriptions that preserve the basic properties of a quantum hydrodynamic description. We've designed a specific kernel that maps random classical hydrodynamic fields to random quantum hydrodynamic fields and demonstrated that this kernel's properties lead to the formation of a gap in the spectrum of perturbations in quantum hydrodynamic modes, a phenomenon observed in sound mode instabilities. Additionally, we've found that this gap arises from the interplay between quantum effects and the random classical hydrodynamic source term and that it could be observable in upcoming experiments with ultracold atom experiments. Ultimately, our approach paves the way for studying the effects of quantum fluctuations in nonequilibrium situations and provides a framework for evaluating the validity of classical hydrodynamic descriptions in quantum systems.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.

The theory of edge localized modes (ELMs) is challenged by the appearance of palm tree modes (PTMs) in inertial confinement ELM-suppressed regimes in the JET tokamak. PTMs are inherently difficult to understand because they occur during periods of low edge turbulence and are often accompanied by massive particle fluxes to the wall. This work explains the origin and characteristics of PTMs by analyzing JET data from the NPA phase-imaging system and associated models of edge dynamics. It is discovered that PTMs arise from a specific interaction between a low-frequency mode and the edge trench, which causes a sudden diversion of particles to the wall, matching the observed large particle fluxes. Furthermore, the relationship between the frequency of the mode and the edge trench is used to identify a potential link between PTMs and ELMs, specifically that PTMs may serve as an early warning indicator for major ELMs, which could have implications for future experiments in the ITER device.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for mobile robots moving at constant speeds in a static environment, addressing this issue using dynamic vortex potential fields in a collaborative approach. By applying this method, a group of robots can navigate around each other smoothly. The proposed dynamic vortex field is derived from Laplace's equation, ensuring it has a unique solution that can be efficiently calculated using a near-identity transformation. This yields a simple and efficient algorithm for resolving collisions. A robust feedback control system is developed to track the potential field, ensuring the stability and continuity of the robots' movement. A comparative analysis of the proposed method's performance is also provided through simulation and practical implementation tests.

Consider a long sequence of letters generated from an underlying source mixture, where the letter combinations are associated with probabilities. Given a fixed large neighborhood size, our results show that the probability of observing a specific letter distribution within this scope follows a typical asymptotic form. This asymptotic form is derived under two primary conditions: one related to stationary data and another to data that changes over time, with modifications applicable to averages over short time periods. In essence, our findings relate the intrinsic properties of the source mixture to the perceived randomness in observed data.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, the IRS has been explored in conjunction with various wireless technologies, including 5G radar systems. This paper investigates the potential of the IRS to enhance radar target parameter estimation by positioning the IRS in an optimal location to modify the incoming radio frequency signal in a specific way. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that when the IRS is optimized to apply a frequency-modulating technique, it can significantly improve the performance of radar target parameter estimation, outshining even the benefits derived from having full channel information available.

Fuzzers are widely used testing tools for robustness testing software, specifically to identify crashes. While effective, they also have limitations and can create difficulties when comparing their performance. The terms "coverage" and "reachability" are often employed to evaluate fuzzer effectiveness yet can have different meanings depending on the context. To address this issue, we propose a precise definition for "coverage" which is supported by a formal model, thereby facilitating a clear comparison of fuzzer performance. Additionally, we introduce novel metrics for benchmarking and competing fuzzers, including those with artificial intelligence technology. Our research demonstrates the benefits of a precisely defined coverage standard through the development of three case studies. Our proposed approach is available online as an open-source project.

Pretrained models have been integrated into continual learning tasks to achieve satisfactory performance levels. However, it's observed that these models often struggle with tasks that have similar features to previous training data. This issue is highlighted in a study involving the BERT-base model on tasks of sentiment analysis and natural language inference, where the findings show that although continual learning methods can assist with tasks that have distinct backgrounds, they still fall short when encountering tasks with similar visual and semantic backgrounds. It's argued that the limitation of continual learning in such situations stems from the expectation that the pretrained model would naturally generalize to tasks with similar features, but this expectation is deemed unrealistic. A novel approach is then proposed by finetuning a single baseline model on the current task alone, without the influence of previous experiences. This approach yields comparable performance to models that have been trained on both the current and past tasks, but it significantly outperforms them in terms of computational efficiency and memory usage. The proposed method is then applied to real-world scenarios in few-shot continual learning scenarios, where it demonstrates improved performance over state-of-the-art architectures in methods like Linear Episodic Return (LER) and GMM-CRE.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces minimizing relative 1-homotopy within a specific class in simply connected metric spaces. Additionally, we establish that when the metric space has a angle condition, its surfaces minimizing relative 1-homotopy are smoothly compatible with rotations.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data have multiple convergent limits, exhibit distinct behavior depending on whether the limits are equal or distinct. If the limits are equal, we previously established the stability of the corresponding equilibrium solution. If the limits are distinct, we previously analyzed the situation where the solution converges to an equilibrium. This article focuses on the case where the solution does not converge to an equilibrium. It reveals that under certain conditions, the solution may converge to a more general form, specifically an orbital neutral equilibrium of the fourth-order Hamiltonian system defined by the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + (fu_x)_x$. It is also demonstrated that this condition is met when the equation $fu_x = xf'(u\pm c)$ is satisfied, where $c$ is a constant. This article also addresses the issue of solutions with initial data that are symmetric or periodic, establishing that under these conditions, solutions that do not converge to an equilibrium solution must converge to an orbital neutral equilibrium of the fourth-order Hamiltonian system defined by the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + (fu_x)_x$.

Recent experimental findings in 64Ni suggest that a peculiar double shape configuration exists, where a spherical 0+ state and an prolate 2+ state coexist. The origins of this phenomenon were investigated using a microscopic shell-model calculation, where it was discovered that the monopole component of the interaction plays a crucial role in shaping the 0+ and 2+ states, and that these configurations overlap due to the large pair-breaking exchange interaction in the spherical 0+ ground state. Moreover, it was found that the monopole component of the interaction is responsible for depopulating the spherical 0+ ground state and promoting the 2+ state to a prolate configuration.

Approximately nine years ago, Arad and Neeman established the concept of lipshitz continuous games as a broader class of games that incorporate a wider range of applications than the earlier broad class of games defined by Bermesky. These games define a crucial connection between economics and mathematics. In economics, equilibria represent optimal states of behavior, while in mathematics, they serve as key points that summarize the underlying geometry of a specific space. However, the relationship between these two aspects of equilibria and geometry remains unclear in the broader class of games, specifically regarding the query complexity required to find an $\epsilon$-approximation of an equilibrium in $n$-dimensional space. This complexity is expressed as $\epsilon^{-d} in terms of $1/d$, where $d$ represents the lipshitz constant of the game. Our research provides the first explicit lower bound for this complexity, showing that it cannot be less than $\epsilon^{-n^3}$, which holds for any $n$ and any lipshitz constant less than $n^2.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification.

Recently, double neural network architecture has gained popularity in knowledge learning tasks due to its effectiveness in mimicking expert systems with limited data. This trend is particularly prominent in student-instructor framework, where a student network learns from an instructor network that has been trained on the original data. Research on this architecture has been diverse, with various names and focuses, however most studies share a common underlying mechanism. This mechanism utilizes two interdependent networks, where one augments the learning of the other, and is therefore a specific instance of architecture that combines two networks working together. Despite its success, this architecture's understanding and potential areas for improvement are not yet comprehensively understood. This survey paper will delve into specifics of the student-instructor architecture, discuss its theoretical aspects, provide specific examples within the context of knowledge learning, and also discuss topics related to its generalization, overall, providing a holistic view of this architecture.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our approach, titled the "Brief Function," enables the precise calculation of a given set of variables' possible values and their associated probabilities within a specified time frame. We have also developed two critical applications based on the Brief Function: first, finding the most probable assignment of variables, and second, identifying the smallest subset of variables that satisfies a given constraint. Our novel variable removal technique, along with a custom engine called the "Brief Engine," significantly boost the efficiency of these computations. In our experiments, our method outperformed existing techniques, particularly on large scales, and showed significant improvement in variable removal and graph manipulation tests.

The interaction between a single laser beam and an ultracold strontium gas was examined at 689 nm, a wavelength that corresponds to an absorption minimum. Typically, this technique is used to study excited state properties, but in this case, we focused on photon-recoil effects. Absorption measurements were compared to a theoretical model that incorporates photon-recoil interactions, and the results showed good agreement, allowing us to determine the one-dimensional photon-recoil shift as $-7.4 \pm 1.6$ kHz. This precision measures the interaction's influence on atomic motion within the optical dipole limit.

When subjected to high speeds of deformation, certain liquids undergo a sudden and significant thickening, transforming into a non-liquid state. This phenomenon occurs in various materials, including rice flour, cornstarch in water, and some industrial fluids. As the rate of deformation exceeds a critical threshold, the material's viscosity surges, often entering a different phase that reacts poorly to further changes in deformation rate. Notably, this transition is not solely dependent on the specific material from which it is made, but rather on the relationship between the material's inherent properties and the properties of the environment around it. Based on the theory that the threshold for shear thickening is determined by a balance of forces involving individual particles and the forces of friction between them, researchers have proposed that the transition should follow a particular pattern of scaling that is not affected by changes in the size of the particles or the fluid's viscosity. This concept is supported by results from a series of experiments using different materials and at multiple scales, suggesting that the relationship between the shear rate and the thickness of the material can be constant and unchanging. This understanding may have implications for the design of materials and systems that involve shear thickening fluids, particularly those operating over a wide range of scales.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. The structure of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is then thoroughly explored through its relation to the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$. Furthermore, all elements of $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed using an recursive approach or by exploring the underlying principles of the higher rank algebra. The centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is found to possess a specific sequence known as the Hilbert-Poincaré sequence, which implies that it satisfies certain properties such as being a semi-simple algebra and having a finite dimension that correlates with $n$. Our study shows that in a bilayer hexagonal magnetic material, low-lying magnetic molecules can exhibit both stability and insulating properties by exchanging quantum forces in a twisted two-dimensional space. Using a quantum computer program that considers the effects of both magnetic interactions and mass imbalances, we found the perfect conditions under which the system can transition into phases of twisted superfluid and supersolid by fudging the parameters of a weak interaction that causes decay. Additionally, we discovered that by increasing the thickness of the two layers while maintaining their tunneling connection, the twisted supersolid phase can emerge from the twisted solid phase, a transformation that could be manipulated by applying external pressure. Our research indicates that it is possible to create twisted supersolid states of matter in a controlled environment, and potential strategies for experimentation and observation in experiments with triplon-emitting $^{3}$He and $^{4}$He gases in twisted bilayer helium.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-nucleus collision velocities-recoil angles distributions and recoil angles-spectra of final state particles. Here, we enhance the visualization of velocity-recoil angle correlations among all involved particles and incorporate WIMP properties, nucleous type, scattering angle, and released energy. The visualization tools will help readers understand the velocity-recoil angle distribution and spectrum data presented earlier.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information.

We are presenting a comprehensive conceptual design for a tev-scale muon collider with multiple purposes. This collider can function as a powerful particle physics research tool, enabling the study of new physics beyond current limitations and potentially revealing the nature of neutrinos. Additionally, it may provide insight into matter-antimatter asymmetry. With appropriate advancements in computational technology, it can efficiently achieve desired results in several areas, including but not limited to, precision measurements of top quark properties, top quark pair production, exotic top quark decays, and heavy gauge boson production. Furthermore, it has the potential to create a vast array of heavy particles such as Higgs boson partners, vector likesons, scalar tops, and vector tops, as well as a variety of dark sector components. It is also feasible to assemble a comprehensive tev-scale muon collider fleet that can tackle a wide range of physics tasks, offering the option for in-depth investigations of specific phenomena in particular areas of the energy spectrum.

A novel approach is proposed to mitigate respiratory motion in standard T2-weighted SE MRI, allowing for accurate comparison of image intensity. A previously established method for tracking respiratory motion was adopted and integrated into image acquisition, utilizing a respiratory sensing coil to trigger imaging at specific phases. The optimal imaging schedule was then identified through data reconstruction, ensuring that images were obtained in relation to the respiratory cycle. As motion varies between patients, it is crucial to individualize imaging in relation to the respiratory position. This study compares two approaches for correcting motion, utilizing two subjects who underwent MRI with an optical fiber sensor to track respiratory movement. Results from two subjects showed that, despite reducing motion correction to a simple linear model, significant improvements were achieved in reducing residual motion. In order to minimize respiratory-induced distortion, it is essential to adjust imaging so that it occurs in the middle of the diaphragm's movement. This can be achieved by correcting for motion during data reconstruction. A novel approach is presented for reducing respiratory-induced distortion in T2-weighted SE MRI. The proposed method involves determining the optimal imaging schedule in relation to the respiratory cycle, either by conducting a preliminary scan or deriving it from data reconstruction. This technique was successfully evaluated on two subjects who underwent MRI with an optical fiber sensor to track respiratory movement.
