In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth.

This R package, lfda, facilitates the implementation of local fisher discriminant analysis (LFDA) across various contexts. The LFDA method is a locally adapted version of the traditional fisher discriminant analysis, tailored to handle datasets with complex structures. The package enables users to execute basic LFDA operations, including dimension reduction, classification, and feature selection. Furthermore, lfda provides advanced capabilities like semi-supervised LFDA, using labeled and unlabeled data to adapt the model, and a visualization function to graph LFDA components. Additionally, the package accommodates diverse data types and allows users to create customized lists for combining extraction functions.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained imitation learning, learning from unlabeled data is often necessary to cope with changing environments, from 2D wheel chair optimization to 3D human navigation. Current methods usually disregard the presence of static or dynamic obstacles in the environment during imitation learning, leading to the derivation of a new method, Extended Kernelized Maximum Likelihood Estimation (EKMP), which addresses nonlinear constraints and obstacle avoidance during unstructured learning. Developed within the framework of maximum likelihood estimation, EKMP is an unsupervised generalization of kernelized maximum likelihood estimation, capable of handling complex constraints and the avoidance of static and dynamic obstacles in a 3D environment, from which the robot can learn during unstructured time periods.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs.

A novel kind of topological superfluidity characterized by spin-polarized vortices and a multipartite entanglement measure emerges in the Rashba Hubbard model, which has an attractive interaction between fermions that also interact with a spin-flipping external potential. This finding occurs across multiple Rashba interaction strengths within the model's superfluid region. Additionally, the Rashba Hubbard model exhibits rapid transitions between normal and superfluid states as the Rashba interaction is adjusted, and this phenomenon is closely linked to the model's phase transition characteristics. A thorough analysis of the model's phase structure is also conducted.

By utilizing the sensitive response of vortex magnetic-field patterns to slight changes in pressure in doped insulators, called the "pressure-tuning curve," researchers previously found that the arrangement of vortices transitions from an aligned pattern to a perpendicular pattern as the density of carriers increases, which is common to all superconducting materials studied so far. However, the underlying cause of this transition is not well understood and cannot be predicted by current theories. In the study of superconducting materials with high $T_\textrm{c}$ values, specifically in the optimized sample LBCO-Opt with a critical temperature of 18 K, researchers discovered that the transition from an aligned pattern to a perpendicular pattern of vortices occurs at a specific carrier-density value, which is distinct from the pressure-tuning curve and does not follow the same pattern. Furthermore, the arrangement of vortices is found to be more complex in optimized sample LBCO-Opt, as it responds differently to changes in both pressure and carrier density. This finding provides a new perspective on the relationship between the distribution of vortices and the unique properties of these materials and suggests that both pressure and carrier density play a role in determining the arrangement of vortices.

The highly stretched state of a grafted polymer brush consists of regions where chain segments are located both near the grafting surface and in the distance from it. Research has focused primarily on planar or semi-spherical brush shapes, with very long polymers displaying distinct characteristics, including an empty region near the edge and a significantly different height. This study investigates brush shapes that are neither planar nor semi-spherical, particularly those that are highly stretched and complex in shape, with particular attention on how an 'exclusion area' at the edge develops when the chains are very long. Using a new approach that directly considers the space occupied by each segment, the theoretical analysis reveals that this 'exclusion area' disappears in very long, arbitrarily shaped brush scenarios.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A minimal identifying set is one with the fewest points. We investigate the concept of using a specific number of points to identify a graph, where a sub-set of k points with the fewest possible connections is chosen to fully identify the graph. We study the behavior of this sub-set when we increase the number of points from 1 to 3 and discuss the difficulties in extending this to more than 3 points.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image analysis, applying it to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To test this approach, they simulated map data containing both machine learning-trained source features and irrelevant map variations. The study showed that machine learning models could enhance the creation of source maps, particularly for sources that change over time and are difficult to identify. Additionally, this technique was effective even with limited training data when modeling spatial variations in source emission. Furthermore, it yielded improvements in source sensitivity in regions of the sky where sources fluctuate significantly.

A serial dictatorship is a method for making choices when there is agreement that cannot be reached, by taking individual preferences into account. It does this by establishing a clear order of choice for the candidates, based on their positions in the order of preference. If the candidates' preferences are known, the sequence of choice can be determined easily. However, things become more complicated when only general patterns of preference are known, as it becomes a problem of optimizing a function subject to certain constraints. This paper shows that if the relationships between the candidates' preferences are clear, specifically if they form a series of connected influences, then it is possible to find the sequence of choice by using a method based on the criteria, despite the complexity of the preferences. This is an advancement, as it makes the most efficient use of the information available when the candidates have a linear ordering of preference. This is achieved without referring to previous findings related to this topic.

We conducted a comprehensive search for binary asters, also known as Mizar stars, within the Pan-STARRS1 point source catalog. These influential stars have a noticeable effect on the motion of nearby O-type main-sequence stars, particularly Mirzam, which is the brightest binary aster in the sky. To identify candidate binary asters, we applied strict filtering to the PSS1 data, utilizing observations from at least three different viewing angles and excluding stars with a recorded spectral type. This resulting list of candidate binary asters was then cross-referenced with existing catalogs containing spectral type classifications. Following this cross-referencing process, we determined that the most prominent candidate binary aster for Mirzam is a contact binary star with a spectral type of BII, consistent with the previously held classification for Mirzam. A discussion on the potential for these stars to exhibit binary characteristics and the potential for more binary asters to be discovered with the VLT/MIRADON interferometer is also included.

This research extends the general partial linear regression model to include network-dependent variables and allows the partial linear component to incorporate an inner regression model. The conditional mean specification incorporates network-dependent variables and is based on the parametric and semiparametric augmentation principles. The study establishes the asymptotic theory for the estimated conditional mean specification and provides an empirical application to examine peer influences within educational networks. The findings suggest that both network-dependent variables and peer influences have a significant impact on student test scores and that there is evidence of unobserved network effects.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives a new type of the Leibniz Rule by applying the parameter variation to the variable-order fractional derivative. Additionally, this study establishes connections to prior forms of the Leibniz Rule and provides examples to illustrate the proposed method.

This paper investigates how complex signals are detected using complex data that varies spatially. The detection method employs an adaptive filter based on a minimum mean square error (MMSE) criterion, which includes the calculation of filter coefficients using the recursive least squares (RLS) algorithm. We establish a theoretical bound on the minimum detection probability based on the signal-to-noise ratio and characteristics of the spatial variance. This bound helps determine the optimal parameters for the RLS algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through simulations of passive sensing and target detection.

We've developed an open-source suite of web tools to support the representation,  model fitting, and visualization of imaging and spectral data using APEX and representational state transfer (REST) services. This suite is part of an open-source framework for building web applications that provide scientific data visualization and analysis capabilities. The tools include various visualization options for plotting data against other data, wavelength spectra, light curves, phase diagrams, and map images. Additionally, users can utilize the APEX Client library, which is a set of pre-built REST services for interacting with the APEX Services. The APEX Client library is part of the framework's API and is available through the GitHub repository.

The Southern Atlantic rift underwent a significant change in opening direction over time, shifting from a narrow zone of extension in southwestern Africa to a broader area in southeastern South America. Models of crustal stretching and rift basin geometry were tested and a new kinematic model was created using satellite imagery and topographic data to analyze the rift's perimeter. The model revealed various radial lengths and patterns in the southwestern African, tropical African, and southeastern South American regions. The results indicated various radial lengths and patterns in the southwestern African, tropical African, and southeastern South American regions. The data suggested that microplate boundaries existed in tropical Africa and southwestern Africa. A new model for the southern mid-latitudes was also proposed, incorporating the Agulhas Rift and featuring counter-opening movements in tropical Africa and southwestern Africa. The model for the southern mid-latitudes was similar to the 500km-wide rift model but with distinct variations in the western and central areas.

A proven strategy to enhance segmentation models through unsupervised training is unsupervised contrastive learning, which pushes similar unsupervised segments towards convergence and pulls distinct segments apart. However, this method's effectiveness relies heavily on the quality of unsupervised masks, which are often derived from segmentation models pre-trained on related labeled data, thereby undermining its unsupervised nature. Additionally, this method assumes that unsupervised and labeled boundary information has the same accuracy, which is not always the case, especially when dealing with medical images with noisy or incomplete boundary information. As a solution, we propose a novel unsupervised learning framework that takes into account the differences between unsupervised and labeled boundary information and uses a unsupervised contrastive learning framework to be presented at the conference, to which we would like to contribute our approach.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

Similar to other cultural aspects, the meaning of words evolves over time to reflect changes in a society's values. What exactly has been said becomes clearer by examining the variations in word usage among different language speakers. This study introduces an initial survey to understand lexical variation discovery, focusing on the analytical aspects of language. It is argued that machine learning techniques can uncover word variations based on their semantic changes, and various methods are presented for achieving this goal. Additionally, a proposed approach for identifying lexical variations through shifted task learning is outlined, along with a preliminary experiment using a historically derived dataset. This research paves the way for exploring lexical variation discovery in speech.

We propose a new approach to understanding the kinematic dependencies of quasiparticle distribution functions within the context of a nonperturbative, quantum field theory. This approach is based on the fundamental properties of a quantum field theory and is independent of the specific method used for its nonperturbative solution. As an example, we apply our method to the Bose-Einstein distribution and demonstrate that it leads to a consistent connection between the quasiparticle distribution and the self-energy of particles. Furthermore, we derive a general integral formula that relates the quasiparticle distribution to the spectral function of a particle, which is a generalised Bose-Distribution.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area of ongoing biophysical investigation. While recent research has made progress in detecting knots in proteins, the study of knot types, specifically in folding states, has yet to occur. By developing novel analytical methods to distinguish and classify knots using gauge space non-abelian geometry, a new approach identifies the types of knots present in the folding states of 9377 proteins extracted from the BONDS database. The results show that simple knots (i.e., trefoils, 5_2 links) are found in folding states at rates consistent with predictions made by the folding funnel model, whereas more complex knots are found in greater quantities than predicted and exhibit different type distributions. Moreover, analyzing the geometry of knot spaces allows for the identification of distinct pathways leading to knot formation in folding states, and reveals that in some cases, multiple knot types can originate from the same starting configuration.

To resolve the problem of unresolved parameters in cosmological studies, researchers often employ assumptions to fix certain variables, yet these assumptions may not always hold validity. Nonetheless, a recent statistical approach, the profile likelihood, offers a way to derive a more precise limit for additional early dark energy without invoking assumptions that might not be physically sound. Utilizing the Planck satellite data and Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey results, the study finds that the power-law index np must be within the range of 1.07 to 1.17 to achieve a suitable cosmological fit, independent of assumptions. Moreover, the study finds that early dark energy can be constrained effectively when np is fixed at 1.1, with a limit of Teff ~ 0.072 at 95% confidence level.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed examination of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is conducted, focusing on its underlying assumptions within a quantum field theory context. The arguments of NG theorem proponents are clarified, and a distinction is drawn between the necessary and sufficient conditions for the NG phenomenon to occur. A step-by-step derivation of the NG theorem conditions is provided, addressing potential ambiguities in earlier publications. The results are then applied to evaluate the NG spectra in both relativistic and nonrelativistic theories, utilizing a 'effective potential' approach that reflects the chosen framework's characteristics. The complexities of NG mode interactions are discussed, along with the limitations imposed by low-energy approximations. The distinctive features of both relativistic and nonrelativistic NG phenomena are highlighted, with a discussion on the potential for NG mode decoupling from the primary system in certain situations.

Reasoning about hypothetical situations requires understanding the consequences of
altering specific components within complex scenarios. Although advanced language models
can process intricate phrases, their ability to reason about these scenarios is largely
unexplored. In this research, we examine a particular set of phrasal hypotheses that
compare an original statement to a modified version. Our findings reveal that two
aspects are crucial for these to hold true: the initial assumption made by the statement
and its underlying justification. We investigate how well these aspects can be
extracted from a range of language models by conducting a series of supervised
and unsupervised evaluations. Our analysis reveals that few existing datasets are
effective in assessing the capacity of these models to reason about phrasal hypotheses.
To address this limitation, we develop the DISCO dataset, a comprehensive test of a
model's ability to distill the hypothetical assumptions underlying complex phrases.
In evaluating the performance of various language models on this dataset, we find
that several aspects influence their ability to pass the test, including sensitivity to
the quantity of available context and the complexity of the statements in question.
Overall, our research provides a clear framework for defining the ability of language models to reason about complex scenarios and highlights the importance of carefully selecting the statements evaluated in such research.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs. Our findings apply to the classes of circulant graphs comprised of the integers 1, 2, and 4, where the underlying circle has at least five nodes. We obtained results for the circulant graphs defined by the integers 1, 2, and 4 on a circle with three nodes, as well as those defined by the multiples 1, 2, 4, and 8 on circles with six nodes. Additionally, our research includes analogous results for the equitable and neighborhood sum distinguishing variants of these colorings.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that the Hf0.5Zr0.5Heusler film exhibits a unique equilibrium, shifting between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals growth mechanisms in relation to the surface energy of graphene, which can be manipulated through the presence of hydrogen. A model is also presented to illustrate the effect of hydrogen on graphenecurvature and the resulting film morphology, providing a pathway for the unambiguous demonstration of remote epitaxy.

This paper delves into the study of $p$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, initially presented in a previous work where the code's rank and minimum rank distance were examined. Here, we continue the study by investigating its dimension and kernel. Similar to the previous findings, a $p$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code of rank $n$ can be viewed as a subset of $V_{n,p^2}^{(p-1)}$, and its dimension is characterized and determined in terms of $n$ and $p$. Additionally, the code's kernel dimension is characterized and has distinct cases based on whether $n$ is even or odd, resulting in simplified descriptions in both situations.

The operation of a polymer flood is critically dependent on the injection profile of a plug containing polymer, as it lays the foundation for efficient polymer use and maximal oil recovery. Based on mathematic models, the objective of maximizing the time-average oil relative permeability multiplied by the saturation should be optimized with the available injection profile options for a specific polymer plug configuration. A novel approach is presented in this work to achieve this optimization through the generation of a linear programming problem in time increments. Additionally, a method for determining the optimal injection profile was developed, as was a way to calculate the polymer injection profile with the aim of increasing oil relative to fractional flow. A numerical example is provided to demonstrate the practical application of this approach.

When dealing with high-dimensional data and complex classifications, it is common to encounter situations where a positive sample cannot be classified independently. In such cases, utilizing additional negative examples related to the uncertain sample can be beneficial. However, using these negative examples individually is impractical due to their extensive number. Consequently, using the underlying structure among these related examples to determine additional relevant samples, or a narrow range within the uncertain instance's neighboring area, becomes a more feasible approach. Based on the theory of manifold learning, which suggests that intrinsically organized data possesses a distinct structure, we propose a novel algorithm aimed at identifying additional samples with multiple labels from a single positive label. This algorithm, which leverages a technique called temporary neighbor analysis to determine the local structure among related examples, can recover the underlying organization within the data by adjusting a key parameter. Through extensive experiments using multiple datasets, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing approaches.

This study investigates the energy bound of a variant of the phase-field equation that has been previously established, specifically the one given in equation (1.3), and demonstrates that it no longer holds no more than $O(\delta)$ as $\delta$ decreases. To overcome this limitation, a newly derived energy bound is shown in Theorem 1, holding the order $O(\delta^{1/2})$, which indicates that the energy limit improves as $\delta$ decreases. Furthermore, this revised energy bound facilitates the convergence proof of the phase-field equation to the sharp interface model formulation in Theorem 2.

The relationship between physical states and observable quantities is governed by the principle of positivistic efficacy, which can be represented as a categorical relationship that generates a category of physical states (S) from a category of observables (O) through a category of effects (E). This connection can be expanded to involve categories of states and effects that form a subcategory of the category of physical states. These state and effect categories are linked by a category of positive operators, which in turn is related to a category of self-adjoint operators. These connections can be represented as a series of 2-categorical relationships that generate a 2-category of physical states (S) from a 2-category of observables (O) through a 2-category of effects (E). This process involves categorifying both the compactness property and the trace property, which are fundamental properties governing the relationship between states and observables.

The source of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting extreme high energies remains a mystery.  A plausible explanation is that these gamma-rays are produced when particles accelerated by mechanisms such as magnetic storms or relativistic jets interact with surrounding matter and magnetic fields.  However, the possibility that gamma-rays are created when particles are confined by strong magnetic fields due to their high velocity and multiply their energy over many times in a process called relativistic feedback should also be considered.  In support of this theory, we found that the magnetic field restriction model can fit observed data including radio wave spectra and velocities from several galaxies and modeling of global electron acceleration in these galaxies was confirmed, providing a key insight into the physics behind this process.  Furthermore, this model may be applicable to a wider range of galaxies as it can fit observed data without conflicting with established theoretical knowledge of these galaxies.

This research investigates how portfolio returns are allocated across different stock categories and suggests developing a new method that draws on econometric theory. We demonstrate this new approach's superiority over established methods using statistical tools. Additionally, the study explores potential real-world applications using economic data.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate sound recordings are necessary for reliable diagnosis through cardiac auscultation.  Environmental and mechanical distortions can severely impact the accuracy of this method.  In this research, a cardiac auscultation method using deep learning techniques was tested against various types of noise and mechanical distortions.  A convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained and tested with a dataset containing normal and abnormal heart sound recordings that were subjected to different types of noise and mechanical distortions.  The results showed that even with significant noise and mechanical distortions, the CNN was able to achieve high accuracy rates of over 90%.  This research demonstrates the potential for deep learning techniques to deliver robust and accurate cardiac auscultation results even in noisy environments.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence issue. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field. 
This process inevitably leads to a chaotic, universe-altering phase shift, likely after several hundred 
cosmological time cycles. Dark energy dominance, therefore, cannot persist forever, and the chance 
exists that we reside in the universe's first epoch. Our quintessence model illustrates the 
dysfunctional universe dynamics resulting from the descent of heavy states, when a multitude of particles 
are produced, overshadowing the quintessence's power. Additionally, our theory raises implications 
for the universe's early inflationary periods.

The rapid evolution of software applications leads to significant issues with maintaining existing tools for software testing and validation. Many tools developed in the past for detecting specific types of vulnerabilities become outdated due to changes in the software environment, rendering them ineffective. To address this challenge, instead of focusing on detecting particular vulnerabilities, this new approach utilizes machine learning to identify anomalous patterns within software code. This method, called Automated Software Processing, leverages machine learning to enable the detection of unknown software threats without requiring explicit signatures or patterns. The implementation of this approach, called Kie, is a Java-based tool that uses a multi-layered architecture to detect patterns within software code. Kie's detection capabilities were successfully evaluated using a dataset of 200 software applications, and it was found that this approach is capable of running at a speed of up to 50 packages per second.

This study explores a complex issue in optimal control theory, where the costs of transitioning between states and the objective function itself change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to develop a method for identifying the optimal control strategy, both with and without constraints on the size of the jumps that can occur.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates unequal leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. With consideration of current LHC data and maximally adaptable standard model predictions, our study finds leptoquark masses below 1250 geV and a specific charge of 1, meeting the condition $m_{LQ} > 435 geV$ when leptoquarks have a charge of 3, and $m_{LQ} > 655 geV$ when leptoquarks have a charge of 5. Our analysis also establishes optimal sensitivities for future 100 geV LHC experiments, predicting $m_{LQ} > 1745$ geV for charge 1, $m_{LQ} > 1225$ geV for charge 3, and $m_{LQ} > 875$ geV for charge 5 under optimal conditions.

This study proposes a novel guided learning approach to capture complex temporal patterns in sequence data. Unlike traditional methods that rely on sophisticated models for explicit pattern extraction, our approach simplifies the problem by transforming sequence data into a one-dimensional signal. We leverage a highly effective method for non-parametric analysis of such signals by leveraging relative positions and inter-sample relationships. By integrating expert knowledge in the form of operator-based networks, our approach enhances predictive models and facilitates interpretation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through experiments using realistic simulation data and actual measurements from a laboratory setting, achieving superior results compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we investigate the practical applications of this approach by exploring various guided learning scenarios with realistic data, resulting in several actionable insights.

We analyze the CIA (continuum induced absorption) lines of chlorine, which are under-stimulated due to low gas temperatures in the molecular disks of galaxies, affecting their absorption at 1.53 $\mu$m. By examining 21 cm line data for 16 galaxies and far-infrared line data for seven galaxies, we quantify the subthermal stimulation of CIA lines and its relationship with other physical parameters of galaxies. We find that the subthermal stimulation of CIA lines is greater in galaxies with lower gas temperatures and mass fractions, as well as in galaxies with slower molecular gas motions. We also find a positive correlation between the subthermal stimulation of CIA lines and the intensity of far-infrared emission from molecular gas, and suggest this could be used as an indicator of gas temperatures in future observational studies. However, using this method as a temperature probe would require knowledge of the chlorine abundance and analysis of related emission lines.

We address the anomalies recently reported in $K$ and $B$ meson decays, specifically involving the processes $K^+	o \pi^0 e^+ 
u_e$, $K^+	o \gamma e^+ 
u_e$, $B^0	o K^0 \epsilon^+ 
u_e$, and $B^0	o \gamma \epsilon^+ 
u_e$. We propose a comprehensive framework to simultaneously explain the anomalies in these decays, making use of a vectorlike doublet with mass $m_V$ and coupling $\lambda$ to the Yukawa interaction between the quark and lepton sectors. We then analyze the impact of this framework on the decay processes and establish the conditions under which it would lead to an enhancement in the branching ratios of the anomalies in question. Furthermore, we establish the most favorable region for this framework to explain the anomalies, given that the mass of the vectorlike doublet is situated within the range $m_V > 1$ GeV.

Levenshtein initially explored a problem involving the sequence reconstruction issue for permutations with the Hamming distance. Given a set of copied sequences of length n, obtained from permutations of a d-element set, with each permutation occurring exactly k times, the task is to determine the minimum Hamming distance between an unknown original sequence and the given copied sequences. The problem of whether it is computationally feasible to find this minimum Hamming distance exactly has been addressed for three scenarios: when n is less than or equal to 2, when n is 3 and the distance between sequences is at least 1, and when the distance between sequences is at least 2. For the first and third scenarios, an exact algorithm has been developed, while for the second scenario, a lower bound and an approximation algorithm have been presented.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand its scope, using a limited amount of data for each family of instruments and then building on that to identify individual instruments. We've developed a protocol for training and testing called "family-first," where we train the system on a range of instruments within each family before moving on to more specific classifications. This approach results in successful classifications for a wide range of instruments with minimal data requirements.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek answers to a limited number of questions, focusing on understanding key concepts, methods, and findings. In contrast, many users who read academic papers are posed with a wide range of questions that remain unanswered. To facilitate more effective use of research papers, we introduce QuestionPaper, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 14,000 questions addressed at answering specific aspects of related research papers. Along with each question, a clear statement of what particular aspect of the paper it refers to is provided. We demonstrate the utility of this dataset by demonstrating how both simple question answering models and more sophisticated models that take advantage of the context of the research papers can achieve high levels of accuracy in answering these questions. Furthermore, we highlight the benefits of using such models as a means of summarizing the content of the research papers.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform.

Consider a junction with $k\geq2$ incoming ASEP channels, each with an initial inhomogeneous configuration and an observer at a finite distance from the junction. We investigate how the velocity of particles in each channel evolves over time, showing that it forms a velocity process that is independent of the initial ASEP configurations. This velocity process is then used to derive new results about the relative velocity of particles in each channel, including its mean and variance. These outcomes are particularly unaffected by the specific starting conditions of the ASEP channels and are instead determined by the mean and variance of the initial position of particles in each channel. These results are further demonstrated in the case of $k=2$, where we derive the mean and variance of the relative velocity, along with the probability of the event that particles in different channels move at different velocities.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We examine a Majorana fermion scenario using a Majorana fermion tunneling between two adjacent sites on a lattice, and investigate its behavior within the context of the Majorana fermion-fermion interaction model. This interaction causes the Majorana fermion to exhibit both periodic and aperiodic tunneling patterns. This aperiodic tunneling is a newly identified consequence of the Majorana fermion's non-antipodal site selection. It leads to an uneven distribution of probability density across the lattice, resulting in varying local chemical potentials and their effects on the tunneling behavior near lattice edges. This interplay between these effects and the tunneling matrix element is shown to significantly impact the model's behavior at low tunneling strengths, before transitioning to a critically unstable phase at higher tunneling strengths. This phase is characterized by unstable aperiodic tunneling and stable periodic tunneling.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This platform can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the project's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of spinor atom-molecule interactions in isolated systems using quantum field theory. Our investigation focuses particularly on the process of atom-molecule conversion, where two identical atoms with the same spin properties and a third distinct spin atom, all of which possess the same energy levels, are considered. These energy levels are further split into two distinct groups due to a difference in the magnitude. Our calculation shows that the interplay between finite systems' properties and quantum mechanics can result in oscillating patterns of atom-molecule formation, and that this occurrence may be exploited to achieve efficient atom-molecule conversion. Additionally, our research explores the effects of laser radiation on these processes and reveals that laser radiation can lead to a significant increase in atom-molecule formation odds. This increase may stem from a process where a pair of atoms with opposite spin properties and distinct energy levels are created from the interaction between two distinct spin atoms, and one of these atoms then changes its energy level to match that of the other atom, resulting in the formation of an atom-molecule pair. This process can also lead to the creation of two molecule pairs, and this possibility raises the question of whether it may be possible to achieve a significant increase in atom-molecule conversion odds through the application of stronger laser radiation.

Our proposed DNA-storage support structure provides efficient support for both data organization and update operations through a hierarchical system, leveraging Garvey-Quaife water sort for both initialization and update operations. This architecture is capable of withstanding deletion operations and has been successfully tested with up to 128 million base pairs. A simple, fast, and robust code is provided in the attached file.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered images, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that involves approximating visibility considerations through visibility maps, which are derived analytically and differentiable, allowing for end-to-end optimization of model parameters. We validate our approach by applying it to the analysis and reconstruction of multiple image-based scenarios, including shape, light source, and camera position estimation, largely outperforming baselines in accuracy.

A prominent issue in interlaced video playback is the interlacing effect, which compromises video quality, particularly in scenes featuring rapid motion. Conventional interlacing techniques fall short in real-time processing for high-definition video. In an effort to address this challenge, researchers propose a novel approach using deep learning, which utilizes video data to establish a reference frame in real-time for motion interpolation. To enhance performance and efficiency, they redesign the network architecture, and to evaluate the method's effectiveness, they conduct experiments using a range of benchmark datasets, comparing its results to existing algorithms. Findings indicate that the proposed technique surpasses conventional methods in both speed and perceptual quality, yielding a mean score that is approximately 5-10% better in subjective assessment and 10-20% better in objective assessment.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.25 fm in the square radius of the neutron distribution between non-relativistic mean field theories and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to differing theoretical frameworks, specifically the formation of the neutron spin singlet and the separation of the convection current from the single particle contribution.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the shallow water equations are simplified to a linear partial differential equation that can be solved efficiently by a Lax-Wendroff method. Secondly, a deep learning-based approach is utilized to train a model on historical flow velocity data, providing a rapid prediction when the solution to the partial differential equation diverges. This combined approach offers rapid river flow velocity predictions without needing exact riverbed measurements, making it an appealing solution for real-time flood risk management.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels.
This technique is readily available on smartphones through a feature called HDR.
Although HDR is user-friendly, manual control over exposure is not available on smartphones.
This research aims to give smartphone users control over HDR by automatically determining the optimal exposure levels for capturing photos.
A novel approach called AEF, which involves determining optimal exposure by consulting other photos of the same scene, has been proposed.
The AEF method yields noticeable improvements in HDR quality, outperforming the standard smartphone HDR functionality.

In our proposed framework, causal deep learning is integrated with the strengths of top-down and bottom-up approaches to create a comprehensive overview of methods combining causality and representation learning. Our exhaustive analysis categorizes these approaches into four key areas, considering both the depth and breadth of representations, and whether learning is driven by top-down or bottom-up processes. Each section delves into the underlying algorithms, evaluation metrics, and key findings related to performance and efficiency. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications and opportunities for future research in causal deep learning.

Achieving uniform and efficient catalytic reactions in fixed bed reactors is essential, but however, temperature distributions within these systems can vary significantly, even leading to temperature fluctuations. Understanding and regulating temperature arrangements are crucial for optimizing reaction rates and prolonging reactor lifespan. Utilizing rapid MRI, we investigated the temperature arrangement in a cylindrical bed filled with iron particles and heated from the outside. Our findings show consistent patterns of temperature decrease from the center to the periphery in the bed, even in the absence of convection. Notably, arranging particles in a packed form significantly reduces axial temperature gradients. Our results also indicate that convective heat transfer plays a more substantial role than radiative heat transfer in this context. Finally, we observed that convective heat transfer can be influenced by the fluid dynamics within the bed, affecting the arrangement of temperature.

This note presents a proof for a specific case of the Mumford Conjecture, which is linked to the boundedness premise and has implications for the field of topological category. The investigation involves new findings in the interplay between geometric and topological properties of smooth surfaces. The argument for the conjecture at a particular surface, noted as $N_{2,2}$, relies heavily on the application of the bounded premise to a related structured map, which is then used to demonstrate a key conclusion related to the category of that surface. The communication of these results will provide an overview of the interconnection between the bounded premise, known as the b-principle, and the geometric and topological properties of smooth surfaces.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

The distribution of eigenvalues for realizable matrices with the property that each row contains exactly one nonzero entry, which we refer to as autonomous matrices, is examined. This analysis extends the findings related to non-crossing partitions initially studied in realizable matrices with orthogonal rows and diagonalizability properties. The focus here is on autonomous matrices with row structures that do not align diagonally, and it is demonstrated that these matrices are closely analogous to certain family-based renewal processes, thereby providing an advanced concept of realizable matrices that goes beyond the non-crossing partition framework.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, storyline development, and post-production enhancements to optimize viewing experience. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, and the advantages and limitations of existing approaches within this field, while exploring promising areas for future research and development.

Users increasingly rely on encryption alerts from browser interfaces, but the effectiveness of these alerts is uncertain. A primary reason for implementing encryption warnings was to encourage users to switch to encrypted HTTPS connections. However, the goal of inducing an optimal security response from users (e.g., activating HTTPS) may not align with their actual perception of security. Consequently, it is crucial to understand users' subjective security perceptions to effectively utilize encryption alerts as a means of achieving this goal. To this end, we propose a novel framework that can assess users' subjective security perceptions by analyzing their response to certification status (trusted/untrusted) and encryption (HTTPS/HTTP). We demonstrated the practical applications of this framework through two certification awareness campaigns, and our results revealed that users' perceptions of security per connection can be as high as 71% for trusted connections, even if the connection is unencrypted. Furthermore, we observed that users' perception of insecure connections can be as low as 28%, which could imply that users overestimate the security of encrypted connections and underestimate the insecurity of unencrypted connections. Our findings have significant implications for the implementation and effectiveness of encryption alerts, and we believe they will be beneficial for promoting certification awareness among website users.

Recently, highly refined acoustic nanogratings and metagratings have been intricately designed and their exceptional performance demonstrated, albeit only at mid-frequency ranges. This research takes the design a step further by utilizing two-photon lithography to develop novel acoustic metagratings capable of operating at ultra-high frequencies. The designed structure, composed of sub-wavelength units, utilizes a hybrid approach combining geometric restriction and resonant phenomenon to achieve high-frequency diffusion-like behavior. The successful functioning of this design is verified by numerical simulations, showing that it efficiently redirects both normally incident and obliquely incident waves with high precision, especially at frequencies exceeding the acoustic spacings between the sub-wavelength units. This groundbreaking research paves the way for further exploration of acoustic metagratings in extremely small scales and potentially expands the application of such structures in critical environments requiring ultra-high frequencies.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between modes in optical resonators and waveguides. The framework is highly versatile, allowing it to address various applications including photonic crystal structures, nanograin suspensions, and conventional waveguides. Key concepts such as mode interaction, scattering, absorption, and phase modulation are explored through mathematical expressions derived from a general approach. These expressions can be tailored to suit specific situations, thereby uncovering underlying principles that can be applied across a broad spectrum of situations. Furthermore, the theory is robust enough to handle situations where some modes are in the gap and can leverage symmetry properties to simplify calculations, even going as far as providing approximate close-form solutions for some situations.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic stability, enclosing sets, and control policies in systems that can be positively controlled, and we provide converse theorems for linear, affine, and feedback control systems with unbounded controls.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed, high-resolution images from low-resolution images collected by particle image velocimetry (PIV) in turbulent flow. Researchers demonstrated that this method can effectively generate high-resolution velocity fields and associated Reynolds stresses, enstrophy, and vorticity maps at different Reynolds numbers. The model's performance was validated by comparing reconstructed images to actual measurements and found to be comparable, showing little error in velocity correlation coefficients, Reynolds stresses, and vorticity map standard deviations. Furthermore, the model highlighted distinct differences in turbulent structure as Reynolds numbers increased.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding my previous comments made on the wave formula in quantum theory. It specifically clarifies the importance of the wave formula in quantum theory and explains why it cannot be derived from the principles of uncertainty principle alone.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural networks often fall short in this requirement due to their complex decision-making processes. A key factor contributing to this issue is the limited understanding of how input data affects model predictions. In response, researchers have developed various methods to handle uncertainty in predictions, especially those utilizing density functions such as softmax. Despite the success of these techniques, several challenges remain in predicting model confidence, including exponentially high dimensional uncertainty spaces and the limitations imposed by the model's architecture. To address these difficulties, we present a novel approach that significantly reduces the size of uncertainty spaces and learns key energy functions from data to predict model confidence. Notably, this approach is open-world, meaning it can learn from both correct and incorrect predictions. Our method is designed for general use, testing its performance across multiple datasets and models. Our findings show that the methods we developed can learn energy functions that are consistent with human judgment and can be applied to both classification and regression tasks. Our code is available online.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

Understanding business processes relies heavily on process mining, which can be categorized into explicit and implicit process analysis. Explicit process discovery focuses on constructing a specific process model using actual process data, whereas implicit process analysis involves discovering a set of relevant processes that meet certain criteria, often expressed as conditions for suitability. We introduce a novel approach called DeclMin, an algorithm designed to find processes that meet certain criteria by analyzing event data and declaring processes suitable for further exploration. DeclMin uses a declarative model that can handle complexities such as choice, loops, and restrictions, and initializes a score for each possible process by evaluating its feasibility based on actual process data. As more events become available, DeclMin refines its assessment of each process by considering its level of completion, resulting in a more precise ranking of suitable processes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DeclMin with real-world data and evaluate its performance on declarative process models.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths, a phenomenon we term the "reentrant delocalization shift". This occurrence is specifically related to states within tight quasiperiodic recurrences. These findings provide significant insights into the interplay between quasiperiodic modulation strength and dimer interaction in determining wave propagation behavior.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering a 84 square degree field of view, Liger consists of 39 individual detectors that gather optically diverse data, requiring a unique approach to handle its complex signal output. A data processing system, designed to manage the signal at an equivalent of 4 gigabits per second, will interface with the device using a custom communication protocol. To facilitate seamless communication between the device and data processing system, software interfaces will be developed utilizing both the current architecture and proposed new interfaces for the AO system.

A major limitation in the scalability of quantum computing and advanced communication systems is the difficulty in measuring the entangled quantum states of multiple modes. To overcome this limitation, researchers have been exploring the demonstration of entanglement in two-dimensional channels using bi-photon systems. A crucial component in such applications is a device that can separate the spatial modes of two photons, a function typically achieved through a high-resolution lens. However, the resolution of such a system is inherently limited by the square root of a mathematical constant by an amount proportional to the focal length of the lens. A new study presents a novel method using a lensless system based on a binary optical array, which significantly improves the super-resolution by a factor of 6-8, making it a more viable option for applications requiring multi-mode entanglement.
This paper investigates both algebraic and analytic extensions of moduli spaces of analytic functions from a domain in the complex plane to a given variety.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the specific timeframes over which subtle transients become distinct is crucial. This research extends the concept of a two-timescale ecosystem model, originally presented in (Bertoni and Gomatam, 2002), by which the model's equations are reworked to clearly reveal the underlying differential equation framework. The resulting analysis provides a detailed examination of the model's behavior during transient phases and its subsequent steady-state equilibrium. The study also reveals that in regions between stable population niches, early warning indicators of significant population changes emerge within a short timeframe of approximately one generation period.

We investigated the underlying causes of the slowing down of star formation rate at high mass values ($\rm M_*$) in the relation between mass and star formation rate. To do this, we used new insights from a study on the MIR color of galaxies by Mousset et al. (2019), where Mirko Boquien explained how reflected dust emission affects observed MIR colors. Using data from the PAWS sample and BAND magnitudes, we determined the conversion from MIR colors to the reflection fraction $f_{\rm ref}$, demonstrating how $f_{\rm ref}$ increases with $\rm M_*$ in an almost linear fashion. Furthermore, we established a similar correlation between $\rm M_*$ and the ratio of nuclear to total luminosity ($f_{\rm nucl}$), where $f_{\rm nucl} \simeq (f_{\rm ref} - 0.5) \times (1 - e^{-0.15 \, f_{\rm ref}})$. We discovered that nuclear regions contribute a growing amount to the total luminosity at higher $\rm M_*$, which aligns with observations of multiple galaxies using ScienceView. Additionally, we found that nuclear regions have a much faster star formation rate compared to their mass, challenging the fundamental plane of galaxy evolution. Moreover, we found that nuclear regions are more heavily obscured by dust, which may be related to the presence of supermassive black holes

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across different languages, using a multilingual dataset translated from English. Our primary objective is to classify the sentiment as positive, negative, or neutral across six languages - it can also be achieved without translation, using the original English dataset. To solve this problem, we employed various multilingual models and established several single-language and cross-language models to compare their performance. The results showed that using language-specific models yielded better results than cross-language models, while the best cross-language model outperformed the baseline sentiment analysis model in English. Furthermore, we discovered that the ease of learning other languages varied significantly among different models and across different levels of data availability.

Exceptional handling in programs can result in data conflicts requiring explicit repair. Our novel approach, developed for the GPGAS concurrency model, includes self-downgrade and self-invalidations to address repairs. We have established the safety and liveness properties of this approach and shown its efficiency can lead to significant performance improvements. Our model and exception handling technique may provide insight for improving concurrent programs beyond GPGAS.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(f)\left(B^{H}\right)(A)$ has a non-empty interior or positive Lebesgue measure. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(f)\left(B^{H}\right)$, particularly proving that if the density function $f^{H}$ is nonzero at a point $\left(x,y\right)$, then the parabolic box $\Pi\left(x,T\right)$ has a nonempty interior.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield predictable outcomes, including the development of quantum disordered states and characteristic H\'enon-Heiles behavior.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with the potential to predict COVID-19 patients' severe conditions. If accurate, using X-ray images for early risk assessment could be a game-changer. Despite the promise, existing research has only focused on diagnosing severe cases or underlying diseases through image features, without exploring the capabilities of X-ray images for identifying factors that influence ICU admission. Our investigation aims to discover hidden patterns in X-ray images that may indicate COVID-19 patients' need for ICU admission. If successful, this could provide a non-invasive, underlying disease-agnostic solution for identifying patients at risk of critical conditions.

The universal simplicial collection, initially defined by R. Berman in his paper on K\"ahler geometry, has been shown by him to be equivalent to a simplicial automorphism of the algebra representing rational functions on a polynomial algebra. Building on this, we establish that the universal simplicial collection can be identified as a simplicial version of the affine linear group, $Gl_n$. This determination extends a previous discovery by J. Hennion and A. Thomas, demonstrating that the universal simplicial operation can be expressed through the simplicial Lie algebra algebra structure, in accordance with the Hall-Mitchell conjecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the universal simplicial collection can be regarded as a simplicial version of the general linear group $Gl_n$ by establishing a direct connection between the simplicial collection and the simplicial automorphisms of the algebra representing polynomial functions on a free algebra. This connection allows us to demonstrate that the universal simplicial collection can be identified as a simplicial group by utilizing a connection to the simplicial Lie algebra structure, in accordance with the Hall-Mitchell conjecture.

The accuracy of Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) has been impeded by excessive false positives in current models, limiting their application. These models often confuse relationships and interactions between objects, typically addressing this issue by incorporating additional information. However, it is observed that the primary issue lies in incorrectly assuming that certain pairs constitute a specific relationship, concealing a more critical problem of excessive false positives. In our research, we acknowledge this as a multi-head classification challenge, incorporating a simple yet effective approach that concurrently addresses all possible relationships simultaneously. By introducing a distinct object-classification head for each possible relation between classes, we significantly reduce false positives. This approach is computationally efficient and facilitates learning for the classification head by sharing features with the existing single-target object detector. Evaluations on two prominent VRD datasets, Visual Genome and Visual Relationship Detection Dataset (VRDD), demonstrate the efficacy of our method in enhancing accuracy and reducing false positives. Our research showcases a promising path for enhanced VRD performance through the elimination of excessive false positives.

This study offers a supervised action recognition classification model called R-BERT, which is designed to operate with limited and poorly lit video data. The proposed R-BERT is a variant of the BERT model, where each BERT component is complemented by a new delta sampling algorithm that prioritizes optimized class representations over classification accuracy. The proposed method is tested on the ARID dataset, an recently established benchmark for action recognition in low-light conditions. The results show that R-BERT outperforms existing models for action recognition in low-light conditions.

This paper proposes a novel concept called Content-Addressable Concurrent Processors, where the central unit of computation consists of interconnected memory cells that can both store data and program instructions. This architecture allows for simultaneous execution of multiple instructions by different memory cells. We have successfully implemented a Content-Addressable Concurrent Processor using a Field-Programmable Gate Array. Our design employs a simple and efficient architecture that can perform arithmetic and logical operations on two inputs, and we have written a basic program to calculate the factorial of a number using this FPGA-based Content-Addressable Concurrent Processor.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution.
