Certain constraints on the model's parameters are derived from considerations of a radiation-dominated era and the cosmic microwave background period. The model then predicts a constant density period followed by a transition to an adiabatic dark energy state. With eleven parameters, the model is implemented in a numerical code and used to calculate a best-fit solution, matching observed values for the Hubble constant and expansion rate at the present time. Alternatively, a fourth-order transition curve can be employed to describe the model's behavior.

In small group learning environments, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creative confidence, effective communication, and a desire to learn lasting new skills. Unfortunately, little research has been conducted to date on the dynamics of curiosity in these settings, primarily due to the absence of suitable methods for collecting and analyzing data. To address this gap, we have developed a new, integrated approach involving both quantitative and qualitative assessments to simultaneously examine state and trait aspects of curiosity in small group learning settings. This approach is highly versatile and can be adapted to suit the specific goals and frameworks of various studies. We have previously tested this approach in a single study, and the results included the development of a theoretical model explaining the relationships between cognitive styles, learning motivation, self-efficacy, emotional intelligence, and the cognitive and motivational components of curiosity in small group learning environments. The theoretical model demonstrated good fit with the collected data, and the associated variables and constructs were found to be relevant and practical for future applications. We have also included our approach in a step-by-step guide for the benefit of the broader research community.

This research introduces a novel Gaussian process model, centered on Mat\'ern principles, that can be effectively applied to complex datasets incorporating temporal and spatial coordinates. By leveraging the concepts of isotropic stability and consistent kernel functions, we demonstrate that a specific class of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes can be seamlessly integrated onto graphs. Furthermore, we develop an accurate and efficient methodology for training these models, using maximum likelihood estimation. In addition, we demonstrate the accuracy of our approach through explicit proof of convergence and theoretical bounds on model performance. Additionally, we illustrate the practical benefits of our method through engaging examples and a comprehensive comparison with existing methods.

Optimal detection of urban road performance can be challenging due to the limited and unbiased nature of available data. We propose an innovative method to estimate urban road conditions based on rideshare driver reports, leveraging a large pool of affiliated vehicles that regularly traverse the city. Our approach utilizes Bayesian inference to evaluate the effectiveness of driver reports, considering factors such as driver behavior and network manipulation. We test this method in San Francisco, utilizing a large dataset of 3,000 drivers and estimating the performance of over 13,000 roads across the city. Our results show that the proposed system can accurately identify roads that require attention and prioritize the optimization of road conditions for free flow speeds, runoff, and air quality. A secondary analysis examines the influence of various driver characteristics on detection accuracy.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) method as a dimensional domain-independent variation of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). While traditional MSSA can be viewed as conducting SSA on multiple time series simultaneously, MFSSA extends this concept to sequences that are functions of several variables. The development of MFSSA allows for the application of SSA principles to functions across various dimensional spaces, making it a more versatile analytical approach. The effectiveness of MFSSA is demonstrated through analytical and numerical tests, and it showcases greater efficiency compared to combining multiple SSA operations. Furthermore, MFSSA is implemented in R for practical application purposes.

Deep learning-based automated emergency systems have been introduced to enhance road safety by promptly responding to markings and signs, yet surprisingly haven't been extensively analyzed for vulnerabilities until now. Our research uncovers the flawed reliance of these systems on isolated training data and the inadequacy of their design, making them prone to significant errors. Specifically, we demonstrate that at intersections, they become confused by newly painted cyclical markings, and elsewhere they misinterpret newly added pedestrian warnings. Moreover, we reveal that their narrow focus on specific configurations makes them blind to alternative setups. Our findings also raise concerns that these systems could be tricked into issuing non-existent alerts, and potentially even leading to dangerous situations. To address these issues, we propose the use of stateless models that can adapt to varying setups, and we showcase the efficacy of our approach by successfully navigating the challenges faced by these systems.

The global persistence of a one-dimensional random walk is a quantity of interest that has been extensively studied in recent years. It represents the proportion of time the walk spends more than a certain distance away from its starting point. This work builds on that by adding an external influence and then investigating the geometric local time of the walk, finding that it leads to a related persistence statistic that can be analyzed rigorously. The relationship between the geometric and regular persistence statistics is the main focus of this study. It is demonstrated that when the walk is subject to an external influence, the geometric persistence statistic is equal to the regular persistence statistic minus an equivalent quantity that arises from the walk's internal dynamics. This connection between geometric and regular persistence statistics is the key advancement of this study. It provides a new perspective on regular persistence statistics, showcasing their connection to the walk's internal dynamics. The theoretical findings of this study are supported by numerical simulations. A score of 0.37 is derived for the critical exponent of the geometric persistence statistic, a value that is greater than previous estimates for the regular persistence statistic. The methods employed in this study involve a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, including multiple-scale analysis, the use of the Wiener-Chintschin theorem, and extensive simulations of random walks subject to external influences.

The IShTAR plasma source is currently being developed for use in the next-generation ion source for the neutral beam injection system at JET. This plasma source, which employs a helicon plasma generation method, is undergoing testing to validate its performance in a vacuum chamber similar to the actual application environment. The results of these tests show that the source can produce a plasma density of approximately 1 x 10^11 particles per cubic meter when operated in the helicon mode, which is consistent with the theoretical maximum density expected in this configuration. In addition, the data indicate that the plasma density can be regulated by adjusting the power input to the source, with no significant limitations observed in terms of current, when compared to the predicted behavior. These findings provide a solid basis for the development of the new ion source, which is scheduled for installation at JET in 2025.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced computer algorithms to assist with nucleus segmentation, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive. However, conventional approaches typically focus on producing precise pixel-level differences rather than directly producing segment masks, which can be messy and less accurate than expert pathologists. In response to these limitations, a new approach called W-Net has been proposed, breaking the classification challenge into two distinct stages. In Stage 1, a simple dataset with clean backgrounds is created by extracting nucleus regions from the original image, followed by nucleus segmentation based on this dataset. In Stage 2, a convolutional neural network (CNN) is used to accurately identify and count individual cells within the extracted regions. Notably, W-Net bypasses the complex image-to-object-classification problem by dividing it into two more manageable tasks, namely object detection within a clean dataset and subsequent object mapping. As a result, W-Net exhibits superior cell counting and segmentation performance compared to directly mapping images to object classes, as demonstrated by its high accuracy in various experiments.

Let's consider a non-archimalian global field of characteristic not 2. For each of the following groups, determine if a local version of the density theorem holds: (a) $2$-Shtukov's conjecture regarding the density of $G_{2}(K_v)$-orders and (b) $1$-Shtukov's conjecture regarding the density of $SO_{3}(K_v)$ and $Sp_{3}(K_v)$-orders. This paper explores extensions to $SO_{2n+1}(K_v)$ and $Sp_{2n}(K_v)$ in a global field. Additionally, it investigates the local density theorem for $G_{2}(K_v)$, $SO_{3}(K_v)$, and $Sp_{3}(K_v)$ in a global field. The paper also discusses connections to $1$ and $2$-Shtukov's conjectures.

A graph G is considered traceable if every vertex is visited exactly once during a Hamiltonian path. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between a graph's hamiltonian path index (hpi) and its repeated line graph Rl(G). Specifically, we prove that if Rl(G) has an hpi of two, then G must have an hpi of three or less. Additionally, we provide a counter-example to show that the converse is not always true.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory medications, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, necroptotic cell death. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the impact of external factors on the reward signal in reinforcement learning is established, and this is demonstrated through the application to a widely used reinforcement learning benchmark.

A blockchain-based smart contract is a complex program with inherent risks, making timely validation crucial. Refinement types have proven effective in validating the behavior of various programming languages by accurately capturing a program's semantics and ensuring its safety. By combining refinement types with sequential and recursive patterns, this validation tool can accurately assess the correctness of Tezos smart contracts written in Michelson, a pure and functional language. Additionally, a user-friendly interface is provided to assist with the refinement type declaration process. How the tool works, its syntax, and its features are discussed in detail in this article, with a demonstration using a real-world application.

Deep Neural Network structures, such as Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental concepts due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner workings of GCNNs, reinterpreting their operations as a form of matched filtering to provide a cohesive and intuitive framework, simplifying the underlying mathematics. Through this intuitive approach, we pinpoint the critical factors that GCNNs leverage to extract valuable information from data sets, namely, the graph structure and input features. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this framework by applying it to analyze other neural network structures, such as Residential Code Detection Network, and the reputation system in Structural Learning, leading to the development of a novel technique called Time-Difference Analysis, capable of identifying the temporal preferences embedded in sequences.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be observed through a Chern-Simons term in its action. The process is then applied to treat rotating black holes and solitons with gauge fields, and the outcome is a "hairy" solution. The presence of an incoming gravitational wave is used to test the solution's stability. The wave's initial representation shows a soliton structure in both static and rotating scenarios. However, as time passes, the soliton starts deforming and eventually breaks into two distinct objects: another soliton and a traveling black hole. The traveling black hole possesses a rotating hairy structure and a scalar field that matches the initial conditions. In contrast, the soliton experiences an increase in mass due to the absorbed energy from the wave. The process is governed by the ratio of the absorbed energy to the soliton's mass, as well as the rate at which the soliton's mass changes. The solutions and the wave's interactions can also be influenced by the charge on the soliton and the strength of the self-correcting process.

The proposed concept of non-reversible symmetry is explained, along with its underlying theory. Non-reversible symmetry occurs when a reversible transformation meets specific criteria, involving an unusual parabolic matrix that sets the stage for a discussion about the Branes framework. The connection between the Branes group, obtained through hyperbolic extensions of parabolic subgroups, and the non-reversible symmetry group is explored. A simple example from the Branes dataset, specifically Branes 13, is used to illustrate the relationship between the Branes group and non-reversible symmetry. A new classification for the Branes datasets is presented, based on the non-reversible symmetry concept.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral measurement. The inferior performance of lateral direction is mainly attributed to the limited spatial resolution aided by the limited lateral field-of-view (FOV) of conventional ultrasound sensors. To overcome this limitation, a novel Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) ultrasound sensor has been introduced. The VSSA sensor possesses several advantages, including enhanced lateral resolution, increased effective lateral FOV, and the capability to operate with lower center frequencies. The VSSA-based elastography system shows significant potential to increase the accuracy of pathology detection.

We're introducing a new method for coding algorithms, which we call logical pseudocodes, as a means to bridge the gap between computational and logical perspectives on programming. By utilizing functional programming principles and incorporating computation-based interpretations, these logical pseudocodes can be seen as a type of functional programs that can be closely linked to proofs validated through computation. This approach can be seen as a computational implementation of Godel's Dialectica interpretation, allowing us to derive our pseudocodes from proofs in a type theory based on Church's theory, and demonstrating the feasibility of our approach through the development of a functional programming language called Luminus. Luminus combines elements of Turing machines with continuous functions to define computations as total functions, rejecting Intuitionistic Arithmetic with Quantifier Free Sigma one inequalities. We also examine our method by reconstructing several well-known algorithms within the Luminus framework.

The concept of a Ramsey character originates from Ramsey theory, indicating the smallest number of colorings required to distinguish a specific pattern in a uniform setting. This paper explores this idea in the context of Boolean lattices, focusing on V-shaped posets and their Ramsey characteristics with respect to increasing and decreasing functions. Our arguments reveal that the Ramsey character for an increasing/decreasing V-shape with height $n$ and base width $m$ is $m2^{n-1}$, a value that doesn't depend on the order of $m$ and $n$. Furthermore, we establish a link between the Ramsey character of V-shaped posets and the Ramsey number in the Boolean lattices, establishing a lower bound for certain Ramsey numbers in this context.

In the context of Euclidean space, a $k$-centers clustering problem can be defined as a task where we select $k$ balls with the lowest volume, centering them at points $c_1, c_2,..., c_k$, such that they cover the given dataset $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$. The objective is to minimize the total volume of these balls. It has been established that a static $k$-centers clustering solution can be found through the Shamos-Tornqist algorithm in $O(kd)$ time. However, the dynamic $k$-centers version of the problem lacks an optimal algorithm with a strong lower bound, although it has implications for other problems like the farthest point first algorithm. We present a new algorithm for the dynamic $k$-centers problem that operates in $O(kd^2)$ time and maintains an approximate solution with a volume at most twice the optimal volume. This can result in up to a linear improvement in time complexity.

We introduce a novel class of stochastic escape games to mitigate the lack of effective methods for resolving complex situations in dynamic systems controlled by feedback. These systems comprise multiple moving obstacles that interact with each other and a moving target that seeks to evade them. The obstacles follow a random movement pattern with adjustable probability distributions. Our key contribution is a successful application of nonlinear control techniques to develop a holistic approach to resolving the evasion problem. Specifically, we divide the system into separate components, including the target and independent groups of cooperating and non-cooperating obstacles. We then establish a linear representation of each component's behavior and apply a range of generalized matrix transformations to smooth out their movements. By analyzing the simplified movements, we identify specific cooperative and individual patterns and develop tailored solutions to solve the evasion problem. Our successful solution relies on advanced mathematical techniques, including non-crossing condition proofs, generalized algebraic transformations and non-normalizable quadratic forms.

A likelihood function that is inherently cyclic and nontransitive can hinder the convergence of parameter estimates to their true values, ultimately leading to unstable model performance. This note sheds light on the unspecified conditions for a likelihood function to be suitable for parameter estimation, as set out in the standard for statistical software. It clarifies a crucial set of conditions that must be met by a likelihood function to support stable parameter estimation, specifically convergence at the true parameter values and differentiability. It also explains how these conditions can be fulfilled to ensure the convergence of the maximum likelihood estimator to the true parameter values, thereby validating the estimator. Furthermore, it establishes a formal justification for using numerical methods to find the roots of a likelihood function.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring regular-dose CT images from low-dose CT scans without labeled training data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because it requires synthesizing two types of images and results in increased memory and computing time. In response to these challenges, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently switch between producing high-dose and regular-dose CT images by simply adjusting the learned factor vectors. We have established and validated this method on a large CT simulation dataset and 140 real CT images, and the results show that it is not only simpler and more efficient but also competitively effective in enhancing low-dose CT images.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven dialog understanding tasks on the Dialog State Tracking Challenge series and the MultiWOZ 2.1, surpassing current state-of-the-art semi-supervised and unsupervised dialog understanding pre-trained models.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid spacetime 
that is endowed with a conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric. We first establish a 
relevant identity, and then utilize this to derive a crucial stability equation. 
By analyzing this stability equation, we are able to determine the conditions 
required for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric to remain constant, as well as 
determine the associated eigenvectors. Additionally, this research is an expansion 
of previous studies on ideal fluid spacetimes, specifically those described by 
Einstein's field equations.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across the surface of deformed nuclei. By analyzing the density and momentum distributions, we investigated the structural properties of rotating distorted halo nuclei, specifically $^{42}$Mg, $^{44}$Mg, $^{42}$Si, and $^{44}$Si. These nuclei exhibit inflated sizes and distinct shapes in the intrinsic state. Following angular momentum projection, we observed separated halo structures along the y-z plane and flattened shapes in the x-y plane for $^{42}$Si and $^{44}$Si, whereas $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg displayed extended and bent shapes in the x-y plane. Furthermore, we analyzed collective eigenenergies and transition probabilities in relation to angular momentum projection, specifically examining shape decoupling effects across various nuclei. Our results suggest that $^{42}$Si and $^{44}$Si exhibit well decoupled intrinsic structures, resulting in characteristic rotational patterns, whereas $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg demonstrate more complex rotational patterns due to stronger coupling between intrinsic motions and rotation.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

The vector boson approximation is a well-known technique that simplifies the behavior of vector bosons within perturbative QCD, making it easier to calculate differential distributions for processes involving these bosons. Although primarily applied to hadron collisions with high-energy protons, we have successfully adapted this approximation for muon collisions, demonstrating that the combination of larger intrinsic transverse momentum and higher achievable center-of-mass energies for muons could provide better accuracy in predictions for certain observables, such as rapidity and $x_T$. Our calculations also reveal that the efficiency of this approximation can vary depending on the available energy and the nature of processes being considered.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

Twenty-five years before the famous meeting of Alan Turing, Emil Post, and Kleene at the 1947 Princeton conference, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was honoring the memory of three influential mathematicians and philosophers from the 19th century with a beautiful mathematical concept. This concept, involving a specific type of sentence now known as the Godel-Carnap sentence, played a significant role in Leibniz's development of the idea that the world has an objective, truth-based structure. As the field of mathematics evolved, this sentence became a key tool for addressing a broader issue related to the nature of mathematics. It enabled researchers to investigate the relationship between the concept of a universal system and the inherent properties of that system. This line of inquiry ultimately led to a deeper understanding of the fundamental characteristics of a system that is universally applicable.

This paper formulates the three balls conjecture in terms of monogenic functions, which are essentially the complex extensions of harmonic functions, within the context of Clifford analysis. We then demonstrate the applicability of this framework to polynomial functions by establishing a monogenic three balls conjecture. This involves determining the dimension of the space consisting of polynomials that are zero on the boundaries of three orthogonal balls in $\mathbb{R}^3$. This dimension provides specific information for each dimension $n$ over the real numbers. It should be noted that earlier results by Bergen and Hartz in 1960 already addressed this issue directly on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

The problem of selecting a subset of points for sampling is critical in fields like computer graphics, mathematical modeling, and optimization, which often involve solving systems with constraints defined by the points being sampled. However, determining the most desirable points can be an expensive and complex problem, often involving multiple objective functions that contradict each other. In cases where the points have hierarchical relationships, preserving the original structure after sampling becomes yet another consideration. To address these challenges, a novel method called Sequential Spatially Equitable Sampling has been developed, capable of efficiently selecting a subset of points by minimizing the intrinsic distance between their convex hulls, while also preserving the points' spatial structure. This method is particularly useful for tackling large systems with numerous variables and constraints.

To facilitate versatile robotic grasping, having control over the camera and image interpretation system is crucial.  However, controlling the eye-in-hand camera requires adjusting the camera's position and orientation to maximize understanding and effectiveness.  Until now, it was assumed that controlling the camera required multiple images for optimal positioning.  This research introduces a groundbreaking approach using a single image to train a model that can optimize the camera's position and orientation for better understanding and performance.  This novel method eliminates the need for numerous training images and expands the potential applications of robotic grasping using computer vision in various settings.  The researchers demonstrated the method's effectiveness by training and testing it on a dataset of 2000 images, showing it could achieve optimal performance without training on every possible camera position.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single solution, but rather on estimating the underlying posterior distribution, which represents all possible solutions. This paper presents a new approach using a regularized conditional Generative Adversial Network (CGAN) to capture the posterior distribution's key characteristics, such as mean, standard deviation and mode. To evaluate the method, experiments were conducted on synthetic and real MRI data, as well as image inpainting, image denoisy and bicubic downscaling. The results showed that the proposed approach outperformed existing methods in terms of mean squared error and structural similarity index.

This article examines the concept of locally invariant manifolds in the context of dynamical systems and confirms that in the alpha-laplacian system, no surface exists which remains unchanged under the system's dynamics, with the exception of the case when alpha is greater than one and a half.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is characterized by very short communication distances due to extreme signal attenuation. We propose a novel multi-hop approach to increase the reach of these signals. In our model, we assume a large audience and design a optimization problem to maximize throughput while ensuring that each individual receives adequate performance. This problem is complex because it involves a large number of users with varying distances from the transmitter and transmitter mobility. To tackle this challenge, we divide the optimization problem into two parts, solve the first part using optimization techniques and the second part using deep reinforcement learning. Our results show significant improvement in overall throughput with our proposed approach.

The interstellar medium is home to many variations in the line of sight to pulsars, which cause changes in the scintillation pattern of the pulsar's signal. By studying these variations in the line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16, researchers are working to better understand the structure of the interstellar medium along that line of sight. In a study of 116 spectra from 7 GHz observations, researchers detected 77 regions of scattering and 34 shear layers across the line of sight, with most scattering regions showing signs of turbulence over a scale of 100 AU to several thousand AU. The study also found that the scattering properties of these regions varied widely, with some causing minor distortion and others severe distortion. Furthermore, the study found that the neutral hydrogen along the line of sight to the pulsar is connected to the neutral hydrogen along the line of sight to the Earth, with the Scutum-Centaurus spiral arm contributing significantly to the scattering of the pulsar's signal.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with a generative network consisting of two main components: a pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural network within a WaveNet framework. The model estimates the expanded filter weights based on input audio's spectral characteristics and adapts to untrained frequency ranges, effectively modeling periodic signal components even without explicit frequency mapping. Evaluations of QPNet in multiple scenarios demonstrate its superior performance compared to the original WaveNet in terms of mean squared error and perception-based quality and naturalness ratings.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, integrated with a widely-used morphological analyzer called
Buhman. This integration leverages existing morphological analyses to serve as
bases for annotations, thereby streamlining the annotation process. An
administrator can configure the system to suit various annotation needs by
specifying allowed analysis options. The tool then presents clients with
pre-formatted entries containing proposed analyses, along with associated tags
for further refinement. The system's architecture is discussed in detail, along
with a practical application showcasing the platform's effectiveness in
spelling correction exercises.

As exoplanets are discovered at an incredible rate, the focus is shifting from identifying these planets to studying their properties and behavior. This process is especially crucial for evaluating habitability and potential for life in these celestial bodies. Since observing exoplanets directly is challenging, researchers are using transit spectroscopy and phase spectroscopy to collect data, which is then used to create 1D transit light curves and semi-analytical models of phase light curves. These models can identify key features such as atmospheric composition, temperature, and surface features in exoplanets with conditions similar to those of Earth. However, current models are not sufficient to analyze the complex spectra generated by exoplanets in phase, primarily because existing techniques are not adaptable to varying illumination conditions and the movement of exoplanets through their orbits. Here we present a new approach, a principle component analysis of observable spectra, which can characterize the photochemistry of gas-rich exoplanets and identify patterns in their spectra based on their composition and temperature. This method can facilitate the analysis of multiple exoplanes using a single model and expand our understanding of atmospheric processes in these celestial bodies.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode.

The development of advanced technologies like computer vision has transformed
the way defects are identified on roads. This study demonstrates how a comprehensive
road inspection platform called RoadAtlas can be developed, incorporating cutting-edge
computer vision techniques. RoadAtlas features three major components, each capable
of detecting and reporting different types of road flaws using both image and video
feeds. Its modules are designed to be highly adaptable, allowing them to handle
different road material types and weather conditions. At its core, RoadAtlas has
an innovative workflow that combines both machine learning-based detection and
expert human input to improve the accuracy of its findings. Additionally, the
platform includes a cutting-edge map interface for real-time inspection data
visualization and seamless road condition reporting.

The concept of shadows emerges from the bicategorical interpretation of atrophied functors, specifically those functors from a category of morphisms in one direction to the same category in the opposite direction. This extension of classical ideas about functors and natural transformations gives rise to a mark-like property within bicategories, especially in the context of bicategories with an axiomatic property called coherence. The relationship between shadows and coherent bicategories is the central focus of this research. It is demonstrated that coherent bicategories are characterized by the presence of shadows in a very specific form, which is referred to as the principle of minimal marking. Conversely, it is shown that the presence of a different form of shadows, which are then called marked, is a characteristic of categories that are structurally similar to coherent bicategories. The term minimal marking is used to describe the relationship between marked and minimal shadows. It should be noted that the term minimal marking has already been employed in the context of pre-branching nets, although the term marked shadow is newly introduced in this research for precision.

Our research aims to address the challenging problem of identifying and marking excessive information in images, particularly those that contain both objects of interest and distracting visual elements. This task is key in improving the robustness of computer vision models by focusing their attention on relevant details. Rather than relying on the models' internal state and training data, our approach develops a direct method to estimate spatial masks indicating the locations and formats of visual noises. This method is grounded in a separate dataset that includes annotated images highlighting distracting visual elements. We utilize a contrastive learning technique to train a encoder-only framework capable of recognizing both objects of interest and visual noises in a self-supervised manner. The proposed framework is then integrated into training computer vision models as a multi-task experiment, showing improved performance in terms of accuracy and robustness on various benchmark datasets.

Current Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operate within a fixed undirected and unweighted graph framework, which does not account for dynamic relationships between nodes. This limitation prompts an investigation into extending GNNs to handle directed and weighted graphs, specifically in social influence analysis contexts. A new model, called the Lorentzian GNN (LGNN), is proposed to capture the effects of edge weights and directions on node features by integrating the Lorentzian matrix factorization into GNNs. The LGNN model reduces the number of necessary message passing steps by incorporating a target node's influence on incoming neighbors, thus avoiding the amplification of negative influences. The proposed LGNN model exhibits superior performance compared to existing GNNs in benchmark datasets and real-world applications.

This study seeks to contradict a well-known challenge in structural acoustic optimization, where a phenomenon called modal discontinuity significantly hinders effort by creating acoustic resonances at non-structural vibration points and structural vibrations at non-acoustic resonance points, thereby apparently eliminating the possibility of achieving perfect structural acoustic efficiency through resonance synchronization. Our approach develops a novel strategy to tackle this issue by forming an "inverse design space" in which the structural vibration frequency coincides with an acoustic resonance frequency. The proposed method is then tested for its ability to achieve optimal results in both direct and inverse scenarios.

A new method has been proposed to achieve the steady-state generation of squeezed vibrational states in optomechanical systems. This method leverages the concept of quantum compression, fueled by coherent light, and overcomes the limitation of only observing the effects of quantum compression during the setup time. The model includes a drive that creates a constant flow of squeezed photons and allows for the investigation of a broad range of scenarios, including situations where the optomechanical system operates in the strong coupling regime. The proposed method can also increase the amplitude of the squeezed states through a process known as quantum transfer, and could potentially be applied to multiple types of optomechanical systems, including those based on semiconductors, atoms, and metamaterials.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to paths and entities within a model. The expanded version of the calculus is examined for both validity and satisfiability, with a focus on various key properties. These properties include simplicity, determinism, redundancy, and complexity, with some of these properties applicable to either the validity or satisfiability versions of the calculus. These properties are investigated through multiple parameters, with some being based on the number of entities within a model and others based on the complexity of the formula itself. Some of these properties are addressed by focusing on the complexity of certain operations within the $\mu$-calculus, with further discussion on potential outcomes for more complex variants of the calculus.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When combining the linearized version of gravity with harmonic gauge, it results in the Laplace gauge.  This note explains that imposing both harmonic and de Donder gauges lead to a solvable system for massless particles, whereas de Donder gauge alone only works for the massless scalar case.  Furthermore, it is shown that the harmonic gauge solution can be expressed in terms of the de Donder gauge solution by using the harmonic gauge equation.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and coloring. By examining the notion of polarity, a set of rules, in relation to planar drawings of graphs, researchers have discovered a connection which enables them to determine a maximum number of four-valent vertices allowed in certain types of graphs that contain minors, and this same principle can be applied to establish a condition for having a certain property in their own right, rather than just being obtained from another graph. This study also explores how this concept of polarity can be used with other types of graphs that are four-connected and have a certain property, and shows that by applying the rules of polarity to a specific type of graph, known as a planar map, almost all instances of a certain subgraph can be changed to have a certain property, and this holds true even if the polarity of some edges is changed.

In the Weyl-Wigner representation, phase space trajectories of classical systems are represented by Wigner functions, which can also describe quantum mixed states, particularly those that are symmetric and satisfy certain conditions. A specific type of Wigner function, associated with canonical distributions, exhibits the same underlying structure as its classical counterpart. This function's positive semi-definiteness is ensured by a representation of the symplectic form in a symmetric matrix format, which is comparable to the classical scenario. However, unlike its classical equivalent, the quantum version exhibits oscillatory behavior near points that represent non-exponential convergence to zero.

The concept of negative absolute temperature has been ingrained in quantum theory for nearly a century, with its initial suggestion made by Einstein, Lambert, and Hopf in 1915. The term "negative temperature" is actually a misnomer, referring to a theoretical condition where temperatures fall below zero on the traditional absolute temperature scale, characterized by a negative numerical value. This phenomenon arises when the energy levels of a system become so closely packed that a particular energy range contains no usable states. As a result, increasing energy results in a decrease in population, mimicking the behavior associated with negative temperatures. Over time, the idea of negative absolute temperature evolved from a purely theoretical concept to one with practical applications, influenced by contributions from numerous scientists. Its acceptance was solidified by demonstrations of negative temperature in both classical and quantum systems, including experiments featuring negative absolute temperature photons, negatively tempered atomic states, and even a record-breaking negative temperature of approximately 10 billion Kelvin in a quantum system consisting of paired bosons. With negative absolute temperature now recognized as a viable state, researchers have begun to explore its potential by combining it with other unusual phenomena, such as negative refractive index and quantum chaos, to create novel effects, including negative frequency generation, directly downloadable knowledge, and a novel perspective on energy, all contributed by various experts in the field.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises sums of $a_i$ with weights from {-1,0,1}. The problem of determining whether $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|=\frac{k}{2}|h_{\underline{+}}A|$ for all nonempty subsets A in the integers is solved in this paper. Additionally, new outcomes and inverse results for specific values of k and A are derived.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to determine cancer risk and appropriate treatment. However, accurate cancer detection through image analysis is complex due to varying polyp sizes, shapes, and backgrounds. To tackle this issue, we've developed a comprehensive dataset called UniToPatho, comprising histological images of colorectal polyps annotated by experienced specialists. This dataset includes 1020 regions within polyps, classified into three categories for abnormality grading and four categories for cancer prediction. To train and evaluate machine learning models, UniToPatho encompasses 2640 annotated areas at a higher resolution and integrates features from traditional and deep learning techniques. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these features in predicting cancer with high accuracy. Furthermore, we've investigated several architectures of deep learning in relation to UniToPatho classification and grading. Our research finds that EfficientNet and Atrous Spatial Attention (ASA), a novel deep learning framework, achieve the best results in cancer prediction.

This study focuses on solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems involving smoothly varying material inhomogeneities and a plane wave incident field, with an emphasis on problems characterized by very high frequency values. Our analysis reveals that a conventional finite element method can be modified to provide an efficient solution by adapting to the short wavelength length compared to the spatial dimension, thereby offering a more practical approach for simulating such high-frequency scenarios. The adapted scheme involves a parallel technique using a weakly overlapping domain decomposition method, which utilizes a highly optimized, coefficient-independent solver developed specifically for this project. Our results show that the proposed method can yield significant improvements in computational efficiency, and are supported by numerical experiments conducted on various types of anisotropic inhomogeneities, including those with isotropic components.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of calcium and aluminum in various chondrite meteorites, specifically focusing on the effects of terrestrial ages on their development. The analysis showed a distinct difference in patterns, with younger chondrites (having been on Earth for less than 100,000 years) exhibiting isotopic profiles similar to those of comets, while older chondrites (having been on Earth for more than 10 million years) exhibited profiles indicating additional months to years of exposure to solar winds during their passage through the inner solar system. The findings support a previous theory that planetesimals from the inner solar system experienced reduced accretion of solar winds due to their higher water content, unlike their dry, outer solar system counterparts. The research also provides additional evidence that the matsile (Benenitra) meteorite was only in Earth's atmosphere for a short time.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ lattices, reproducing the known results for the XX and XYZ cases and providing a more general approach using the affine quantum-group symmetry.

Language barriers pose significant challenges in international settings, and the ability to translate languages instantly would be highly beneficial. While advancements in machine translation have made progress, there is still a notable gap in areas involving little to no data availability. This time, the focus is on translating unknown languages based on available data from other languages. Building upon combined models of sequence-to-sequence translation and voice synthesis, a novel approach has been proposed to handle this task. The proposed framework incorporates a voice translation model that learns from parallel speech data and generates target language speech, which is then converted to written text. To evaluate the proposed framework, zero-shot English-Spanish and English-French translation tasks were conducted, and it achieved better results than baseline multi-language translation models in both cases.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime.

Building on the concept of quantum immanents, this study introduces a new class of polynomials derived from double Young-Capelli bitableaux. The specific formula for these polynomials is given by $\text{FC}(\lambda)\psi^\lambda$, where $\psi^\lambda$ can be further expanded into the Schur shifted symmetric formula. By examining particular cases, researchers have observed that certain double Young-Capelli bitableaux polynomials are linked to functions representing central invariants in quantum groups, specifically the $\text{FC}(\lambda)u^\lambda$ relationship. Additionally, this study explores the connection between double Young-Capelli bitableaux polynomials and the quantum immanent basis, establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this study proves that the restriction of these polynomials to classical Weyl group elements results in modified versions of the original polynomials, specifically $\text{FC}(\lambda)\chi^\lambda$.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the easiest scoto-seesaw framework, we determine the parameters that influence the dark matter mass, and subsequently, its interaction strength with the Higgs boson. Furthermore, we establish the conditions for the Higgs vacuum to remain stable across all temperature fluctuations. By constraining the model using dark matter mass in the range 1-10 TeV, we find that the Higgs boson's 125 GeV mass must be within a specific range, whereas the easiest scoto-seesaw parameters can be chosen freely, allowing the neutrinoless dark matter decay lifetime to span an extensive range, from $10^{26}$ to $10^{29}$ seconds. We also find that the Higgs boson's effective mass in dark matter interactions may vary significantly, influencing its search sensitivity in future experiments. Ultimately, we find that in addition to neutrino oscillation, the neutrinoless dark matter decay could provide evidence for the easiest scoto-seesaw model's validity.

We employ exact diagonalization to study a model of weakly coupled dimerized Mott insulators, focusing on the impact of strong spin-orbit coupling on magnetic order. This model features two-dimensional $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixed orbitals and considers 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal ions. Our analysis reveals that the spin-orbit coupling overcomes the on-site crystal field splitting, allowing $e_g$ like behavior in all three series. However, the relative weights of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ states vary depending on the atomic number. In addition, the stronger direct exchange interactions in 4d and 5d compounds lead to enhanced magnetic order at moderate couplings, while the heavier 5d ions exhibit stronger coupling between the two sublattices.

Quantum field theories on geometric spaces undergo a precise change of variables in geometric spaces with specific properties, specifically in spaces with properties defined by certain mathematical theories. This specific change of variables affects the fundamental relationships between these spaces and their corresponding mathematical objects, and it has a distinct impact on the physical principles that these spaces represent. This paper examines the effects of a particular type of transformation, called birational transformations, on the relationship between these spaces and their corresponding mathematical objects, and it reveals that this change of variables reveals hidden patterns in their geometry. This paper also shows that this change of variables has a complex effect on the physical principles that these spaces represent, and it identifies specific conditions under which this change of variables leads to a better understanding of these principles. This paper is significant because it provides a comprehensive overview of the effects of bi-rational transformations on the relationship between these spaces and their corresponding mathematical objects, and it reveals important insights into the fundamental nature of quantum field theories on geometric spaces. This paper is related to another paper that examines the effects of another type of transformation, called wall-crossing transformations, on the relationship between these spaces and their corresponding mathematical objects.

Doctors and researchers need to quickly review numerous X-ray images to monitor the progression of lung conditions, but often they need to view the same patient's X-rays on multiple occasions. To streamline this process, we propose using automatic image manipulation to distill high-dimensional X-ray images into simplified, condition-specific visual representations. This is referred to as conditional image mapping. To achieve this, we combine convolutional neural networks in both an unsupervised and a supervised framework, utilizing example images characterized by specific lung abnormalities. Our research demonstrates that supervised conditional image mapping is a viable method for illness-aware image analysis, offering potential advantages for medical researchers and practitioners.

ViDaExpert is an intuitive tool designed for the interactive visualization and comprehensive analysis of vectorial data with multiple dimensions. It enables users to explore multidimensional data through 2D plots, 3D surfaces, and heat maps, also providing statistical metrics and personalized rankings for data comparison. Additionally, it facilitates the detection of patterns by applying dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA.

This research paper evaluates Newtonian potentials over planar regions quickly by using Green's first identity. By rearranging terms, it computes the potential at a point near the region's boundary quickly, achieving a $O(k^2)$ time complexity when using a fast Fourier transform. Furthermore, it provides an efficient $O(k^3)$ time complexity method for computing the potential at boundary points. These efficient computations can be applied to solve boundary value problems for time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger and Helmholtz equations over planar regions with changing shapes, under the continuity and boundedness conditions.
